<p><b>Scotland</b> (<a href="/wiki/Scots_language" title="Scots language">Scots</a>: <i lang="sco">Scotland</i>, <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Gaelic_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Scottish Gaelic language">Scottish Gaelic</a>: <i lang="gd"><a href="/wiki/Alba" title="Alba">Alba</a></i> <small></small><span title="Representation in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)" class="IPA" lang="gd-Latn-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/Scottish_Gaelic" title="Help:IPA/Scottish Gaelic">[ˈal̪ˠapə]</a></span>&#32;<span class="nowrap" style="font-size:85%">(<span class="unicode haudio"><span class="fn"><span style="white-space:nowrap;margin-right:.25em;"><a href="/wiki/File:Alba-gd.ogg" title="About this sound"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/11px-Loudspeaker.svg.png" decoding="async" width="11" height="11" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/17px-Loudspeaker.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/Loudspeaker.svg/22px-Loudspeaker.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="20" data-file-height="20" /></a></span><a href="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Alba-gd.ogg" class="internal" title="Alba-gd.ogg">listen</a></span></span>)</span>) is a <a href="/wiki/Countries_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Countries of the United Kingdom">country</a> that is part of the <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom" title="United Kingdom">United Kingdom</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> Covering the northern third of the island of <a href="/wiki/Great_Britain" title="Great Britain">Great Britain</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-Stats_1_17-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stats_1-17">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Country_18-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Country-18">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Mainland" title="Mainland">mainland</a> Scotland has a 96-mile (154-kilometre) <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Scottish_border" title="Anglo-Scottish border">border</a> with <a href="/wiki/England" title="England">England</a> to the southeast and is otherwise surrounded by the <a href="/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean" title="Atlantic Ocean">Atlantic Ocean</a> to the north and west, the <a href="/wiki/North_Sea" title="North Sea">North Sea</a> to the northeast and east, and the <a href="/wiki/Irish_Sea" title="Irish Sea">Irish Sea</a> to the south. It also contains more than 790 <a href="/wiki/Islands_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Islands of Scotland">islands</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-Scottish_Executive_20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Scottish_Executive-20">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> principally in the archipelagos of the <a href="/wiki/Hebrides" title="Hebrides">Hebrides</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Northern_Isles" title="Northern Isles">Northern Isles</a>. Most of the population, including the capital <a href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</a>, is concentrated in the <a href="/wiki/Central_Belt" title="Central Belt">Central Belt</a>—the plain between the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Highlands" title="Scottish Highlands">Scottish Highlands</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Southern_Uplands" title="Southern Uplands">Southern Uplands</a>—in the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Lowlands" title="Scottish Lowlands">Scottish Lowlands</a>.
</p><p>Scotland is divided into 32 <a href="/wiki/Subdivisions_of_Scotland" title="Subdivisions of Scotland">administrative subdivisions</a> or local authorities, known as council areas.<sup id="cite_ref-cosla.gov.uk_21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cosla.gov.uk-21">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Glasgow_City_(council_area)" class="mw-redirect" title="Glasgow City (council area)">Glasgow City</a> is the largest council area in terms of population, with <a href="/wiki/Highland_(council_area)" title="Highland (council area)">Highland</a> being the largest in terms of area. Limited self-governing power, covering matters such as education, social services and roads and transportation, is devolved from the Scottish Government to each subdivision.<sup id="cite_ref-cosla.gov.uk_21-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cosla.gov.uk-21">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> Scotland is the second-largest country in the United Kingdom, and accounted for 8.3% of the population in 2012.<sup id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland" title="Kingdom of Scotland">Kingdom of Scotland</a> emerged as an independent <a href="/wiki/Sovereign_state" title="Sovereign state">sovereign state</a> in the 9th century and continued to exist until 1707. By inheritance in 1603, <a href="/wiki/James_VI_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="James VI of Scotland">James VI of Scotland</a> became king of <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_England" title="Kingdom of England">England</a> and <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Ireland" title="Kingdom of Ireland">Ireland</a>, thus forming a <a href="/wiki/Personal_union" title="Personal union">personal union</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Union_of_the_Crowns" title="Union of the Crowns">three kingdoms</a>. Scotland subsequently entered into a <a href="/wiki/Political_union" title="Political union">political union</a> with the Kingdom of England on 1 May 1707 to create the new <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain" title="Kingdom of Great Britain">Kingdom of Great Britain</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Keay_23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keay-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Mackie_24-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mackie-24">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup> The union also created the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Great_Britain" title="Parliament of Great Britain">Parliament of Great Britain</a>, which succeeded both the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland" title="Parliament of Scotland">Parliament of Scotland</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_England" title="Parliament of England">Parliament of England</a>. In 1801, the Kingdom of Great Britain entered into a political union with the Kingdom of Ireland to create the <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland" title="United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland">United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland</a> (in 1922, the <a href="/wiki/Irish_Free_State" title="Irish Free State">Irish Free State</a> seceded from the United Kingdom, leading to the latter being <a href="/wiki/Royal_and_Parliamentary_Titles_Act_1927" title="Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act 1927">officially renamed</a> the United Kingdom of Great Britain and <a href="/wiki/Northern_Ireland" title="Northern Ireland">Northern Ireland</a> in 1927).<sup id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Within Scotland, the <a href="/wiki/Monarchy_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Monarchy of the United Kingdom">monarchy of the United Kingdom</a> has continued to use a variety of styles, titles and other royal symbols of statehood specific to the pre-union Kingdom of Scotland. The <a href="/wiki/Scots_law" title="Scots law">legal system within Scotland</a> has also remained separate from those of <a href="/wiki/English_law" title="English law">England and Wales</a> and <a href="/wiki/Northern_Ireland_law" class="mw-redirect" title="Northern Ireland law">Northern Ireland</a>; Scotland constitutes a distinct jurisdiction in both public and private law.<sup id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup> The continued existence of legal, <a href="/wiki/Education_in_Scotland" title="Education in Scotland">educational</a>, <a href="/wiki/Religion_in_Scotland" title="Religion in Scotland">religious</a> and other institutions distinct from those in the remainder of the UK have all contributed to the continuation of <a href="/wiki/Culture_of_Scotland" title="Culture of Scotland">Scottish culture</a> and <a href="/wiki/Scottish_national_identity" title="Scottish national identity">national identity</a> since the 1707 <a href="/wiki/Political_union#Incorporating_union" title="Political union">incorporating</a> union with England.<sup id="cite_ref-administrative_control_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-administrative_control-27">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1999, a <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament" title="Scottish Parliament">Scottish Parliament</a> was re-established, in the form of a <a href="/wiki/Devolution_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Devolution in the United Kingdom">devolved</a> <a href="/wiki/Unicameral_legislature" class="mw-redirect" title="Unicameral legislature">unicameral legislature</a> comprising 129 <a href="/wiki/Member_of_the_Scottish_Parliament" title="Member of the Scottish Parliament">members</a>, having authority over many areas of <a href="/wiki/Domestic_policy" title="Domestic policy">domestic policy</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> The head of the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Government" title="Scottish Government">Scottish Government</a> is the <a href="/wiki/First_minister_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="First minister of Scotland">first minister of Scotland</a>, who is supported by the <a href="/wiki/Deputy_first_minister_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Deputy first minister of Scotland">deputy first minister of Scotland</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup> Scotland is represented in the <a href="/wiki/United_Kingdom_Parliament" class="mw-redirect" title="United Kingdom Parliament">United Kingdom Parliament</a> by 59 <a href="/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom)" title="Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)">members of parliament</a> (MPs). It is also a member of the <a href="/wiki/British%E2%80%93Irish_Council" title="British–Irish Council">British–Irish Council</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> sending five members of the Scottish Parliament to the <a href="/wiki/British%E2%80%93Irish_Parliamentary_Assembly" title="British–Irish Parliamentary Assembly">British–Irish Parliamentary Assembly</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup> as well as being part of the <a href="/wiki/Joint_Ministerial_Committee_(UK)" class="mw-redirect" title="Joint Ministerial Committee (UK)">Joint Ministerial Committee</a>, represented by the first minister.<sup id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r886046785">.mw-parser-output .toclimit-2 .toclevel-1 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-3 .toclevel-2 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-4 .toclevel-3 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-5 .toclevel-4 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-6 .toclevel-5 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-7 .toclevel-6 ul{display:none}</style><div class="toclimit-3"><meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" /></div>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Etymology_of_Scotland" title="Etymology of Scotland">Etymology of Scotland</a></div>
<p><i>Scotland</i> comes from <span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la"><a href="/wiki/Scoti" title="Scoti">Scoti</a></i></span><span class="lang-comment" style="font-style: normal; display: none; color: #33aa33; margin-left: 0.3em;">code: lat promoted to code: la </span>, the Latin name for the <a href="/wiki/Gaels" title="Gaels">Gaels</a>. <a href="/wiki/Philip_Freeman" title="Philip Freeman">Philip Freeman</a> has speculated on the likelihood of a group of raiders adopting a name from an <a href="/wiki/Indo-European_root" class="mw-redirect" title="Indo-European root">Indo-European root</a>, *<i>skot</i>, citing the parallel in Greek <span title="Greek-language text"><i lang="el-Latn">skotos</i></span><span class="lang-comment" style="font-style: normal; display: none; color: #33aa33; margin-left: 0.3em;">code: ell promoted to code: el </span> (<span title="Greek-language text"><span lang="el" style="font-style: normal;">σκότος</span></span><span class="lang-comment" style="font-style: normal; display: none; color: #33aa33; margin-left: 0.3em;">code: ell promoted to code: el </span>), meaning "darkness, gloom".<sup id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Late_Latin" title="Late Latin">Late Latin</a> word <span title="Latin-language text"><i lang="la"><a href="/wiki/Scotia" title="Scotia">Scotia</a></i></span><span class="lang-comment" style="font-style: normal; display: none; color: #33aa33; margin-left: 0.3em;">code: lat promoted to code: la </span> ('land of the Gaels') was initially used to refer to Ireland,<sup id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup> and likewise in early <a href="/wiki/Old_English_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Old English language">Old English</a> <span title="Old English (ca. 450-1100)-language text"><i lang="ang">Scotland</i></span> was used for Ireland.<sup id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> By the 11th century at the latest, <i>Scotia</i> was being used to refer to (Gaelic-speaking) Scotland north of the <a href="/wiki/River_Forth" title="River Forth">River Forth</a>, alongside <i>Albania</i> or <i>Albany</i>, both derived from the Gaelic <span title="Scottish Gaelic-language text"><i lang="gd"><a href="/wiki/Alba" title="Alba">Alba</a></i></span><span class="lang-comment" style="font-style: normal; display: none; color: #33aa33; margin-left: 0.3em;">code: gla promoted to code: gd </span>.<sup id="cite_ref-Brewer_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brewer-36">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> The use of the words <i>Scots</i> and <i>Scotland</i> to encompass all of what is now Scotland became common in the <a href="/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Late_Middle_Ages" title="Scotland in the Late Middle Ages">Late Middle Ages</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Keay_23-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keay-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Prehistory">Prehistory</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Prehistoric_Scotland" title="Prehistoric Scotland">Prehistoric Scotland</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">For a chronological guide, see <a href="/wiki/Timeline_of_prehistoric_Scotland" title="Timeline of prehistoric Scotland">Timeline of prehistoric Scotland</a>.</div>
<p>Repeated glaciations, which covered the entire land mass of modern Scotland, destroyed any traces of <a href="/wiki/Human_habitation" class="mw-redirect" title="Human habitation">human habitation</a> that may have existed before the <a href="/wiki/Mesolithic_period" class="mw-redirect" title="Mesolithic period">Mesolithic period</a>. It is believed the first post-glacial groups of <a href="/wiki/Hunter-gatherer" title="Hunter-gatherer">hunter-gatherers</a> arrived in Scotland around 12,800 years ago, as the ice sheet retreated after the <a href="/wiki/Last_glacial_period" class="mw-redirect" title="Last glacial period">last glaciation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> At the time, Scotland was covered in forests, had more bog-land, and the main form of transport was by water.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 9">&#58;&#8202;9&#8202;</span></sup> These settlers began building the first known permanent houses on Scottish soil around 9,500 years ago, and the first villages around 6,000 years ago. The well-preserved village of <a href="/wiki/Skara_Brae" title="Skara Brae">Skara Brae</a> on the mainland of <a href="/wiki/Orkney" title="Orkney">Orkney</a> dates from this period. <a href="/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic">Neolithic</a> habitation, burial, and ritual sites are particularly common and well preserved in the <a href="/wiki/Northern_Isles" title="Northern Isles">Northern Isles</a> and <a href="/wiki/Western_Isles" class="mw-redirect" title="Western Isles">Western Isles</a>, where a lack of trees led to most structures being built of local stone.<sup id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> Evidence of sophisticated pre-Christian belief systems is demonstrated by sites such as the <a href="/wiki/Callanish_Stones" title="Callanish Stones">Callanish Stones</a> on <a href="/wiki/Isle_of_Lewis" title="Isle of Lewis">Lewis</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Maes_Howe" class="mw-redirect" title="Maes Howe">Maes Howe</a> on <a href="/wiki/Orkney" title="Orkney">Orkney</a>, which were built in the third millennium BC.<sup id="cite_ref-short_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-short-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 38">&#58;&#8202;38&#8202;</span></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="History">History</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/History_of_Scotland" title="History of Scotland">History of Scotland</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">For a chronological guide, see <a href="/wiki/Timeline_of_Scottish_history" title="Timeline of Scottish history">Timeline of Scottish history</a>.</div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Early">Early</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Scotland_during_the_Roman_Empire" title="Scotland during the Roman Empire">Scotland during the Roman Empire</a>, <a href="/wiki/Roman_Britain" title="Roman Britain">Roman Britain</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Pictland" class="mw-redirect" title="Pictland">Pictland</a></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:182px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg/180px-Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="270" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg/270px-Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg/360px-Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg 2x" data-file-width="427" data-file-height="640" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Skara_Brae_-_geograph.org.uk_-_1274913.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The exposed interior of a house at <a href="/wiki/Skara_Brae" title="Skara Brae">Skara Brae</a></div></div></div>
<p>The first written reference to Scotland was in 320 BC by Greek sailor <a href="/wiki/Pytheas" title="Pytheas">Pytheas</a>, who called the northern tip of Britain "Orcas", the source of the name of the Orkney islands.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 10">&#58;&#8202;10&#8202;</span></sup> During the first millennium BC, the society changed dramatically to a chiefdom model, as consolidation of settlement led to the concentration of wealth and underground stores of surplus food.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 11">&#58;&#8202;11&#8202;</span></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Roman_conquest_of_Britain" title="Roman conquest of Britain">Roman conquest of Britain</a> was never completed, and most of modern Scotland was not brought under Roman political control.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> The first Roman incursion into Scotland occurred in 79 AD, when <a href="/wiki/Gnaeus_Julius_Agricola" title="Gnaeus Julius Agricola">Agricola</a> invaded Scotland; he defeated a Caledonian army at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Mons_Graupius" title="Battle of Mons Graupius">Battle of Mons Graupius</a> in 83 AD.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 12">&#58;&#8202;12&#8202;</span></sup> After the Roman victory, Roman forts were briefly set along the <a href="/wiki/Gask_Ridge" title="Gask Ridge">Gask Ridge</a> close to the <a href="/wiki/Highland_Boundary_Fault" title="Highland Boundary Fault">Highland line</a>, but by three years after the battle, the Roman armies had withdrawn to the <a href="/wiki/Southern_Uplands" title="Southern Uplands">Southern Uplands</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup> Remains of Roman forts established in the 1st century have been found as far north as the <a href="/wiki/Moray_Firth" title="Moray Firth">Moray Firth</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> By the reign of the <a href="/wiki/Roman_emperor" title="Roman emperor">Roman emperor</a> <a href="/wiki/Trajan" title="Trajan">Trajan</a> (<span style="white-space:nowrap;"><abbr title="reigned">r.</abbr>&#160;98–117</span>), Roman control had lapsed to Britain south of a line between the <a href="/wiki/River_Tyne" title="River Tyne">River Tyne</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Solway_Firth" title="Solway Firth">Solway Firth</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:8_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:8-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> Along this line, Trajan's successor <a href="/wiki/Hadrian" title="Hadrian">Hadrian</a> (<span style="white-space:nowrap;"><abbr title="reigned">r.</abbr>&#160;117–138</span>) erected <a href="/wiki/Hadrian%27s_Wall" title="Hadrian&#39;s Wall">Hadrian's Wall</a> in northern England<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 12">&#58;&#8202;12&#8202;</span></sup> and the <i><a href="/wiki/Limes_Britannicus" title="Limes Britannicus">Limes Britannicus</a></i> became the northern border of the Roman Empire.<sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-45">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup> The Roman influence on the southern part of the country was considerable, and they introduced <a href="/wiki/Christianity" title="Christianity">Christianity</a> to Scotland.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 13–14">&#58;&#8202;13–14&#8202;</span></sup><sup id="cite_ref-short_40-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-short-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 38">&#58;&#8202;38&#8202;</span></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Antonine_Wall" title="Antonine Wall">Antonine Wall</a> was built from 142 at the order of Hadrian's successor <a href="/wiki/Antoninus_Pius" title="Antoninus Pius">Antoninus Pius</a> (<span style="white-space:nowrap;"><abbr title="reigned">r.</abbr>&#160;138–161</span>), defending the Roman part of Scotland from the unadministered part of the island, north of a line between the <a href="/wiki/Firth_of_Clyde" title="Firth of Clyde">Firth of Clyde</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Firth_of_Forth" title="Firth of Forth">Firth of Forth</a>. The successful <a href="/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Caledonia_208%E2%80%93210" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman invasion of Caledonia 208–210">Roman invasion of Caledonia 208–210</a> was undertaken by emperors of the imperial <a href="/wiki/Severan_dynasty" title="Severan dynasty">Severan dynasty</a> in response to the breaking of treaty by the Caledonians in 197,<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> but permanent conquest of the whole of Great Britain was forestalled by the death of the senior emperor <a href="/wiki/Septimius_Severus" title="Septimius Severus">Septimius Severus</a> (<span style="white-space:nowrap;"><abbr title="reigned">r.</abbr>&#160;193–211</span>) while on campaign at <a href="/wiki/Eboracum" title="Eboracum">Eboracum</a> (<a href="/wiki/York" title="York">York</a>), and the Caledonians were again in revolt in 210–211.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> Forts erected by the <a href="/wiki/Roman_army" title="Roman army">Roman army</a> of the Severan campaign were placed near those established by Agricola and were clustered at the mouths of the <a href="/wiki/Glens" class="mw-redirect" title="Glens">glens</a> in the Highlands.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To the Roman historians <a href="/wiki/Tacitus" title="Tacitus">Tacitus</a> and <a href="/wiki/Cassius_Dio" title="Cassius Dio">Cassius Dio</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Highlands" title="Scottish Highlands">Scottish Highlands</a> and the area north of the <a href="/wiki/River_Forth" title="River Forth">River Forth</a> was called <a href="/wiki/Caledonia" title="Caledonia">Caledonia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> According to Cassius Dio, the inhabitants of Caledonia were the <a href="/wiki/Caledonians" title="Caledonians">Caledonians</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Maeatae" title="Maeatae">Maeatae</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> Other ancient authors used the adjective "Caledonian" to pertain to anywhere in northern or inland Britain, often mentioning the region's people and animals, its cold climate, its pearls, and a noteworthy region of wooden hills (<a href="/wiki/Latin_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Latin language">Latin</a>: <i lang="la">saltus</i>) which the 2nd-century AD Roman philosopher <a href="/wiki/Ptolemy" title="Ptolemy">Ptolemy</a>, in his <a href="/wiki/Geography_(Ptolemy)" title="Geography (Ptolemy)"><i>Geography</i></a>, described as being south-west of the <a href="/wiki/Beauly_Firth" title="Beauly Firth">Beauly Firth</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> The name Caledonia is echoed in the place names of <a href="/wiki/Dunkeld" title="Dunkeld">Dunkeld</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rohallion" title="Rohallion">Rohallion</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Schiehallion" title="Schiehallion">Schiehallion</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:4_41-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:4-41">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Great_Conspiracy" title="Great Conspiracy">Great Conspiracy</a> against Roman rule in Britain in the later 4th century, in which the <a href="/wiki/Scoti" title="Scoti">Scoti</a> participated, was defeated by the <a href="/wiki/Comes_Theodosius" class="mw-redirect" title="Comes Theodosius"><i>comes</i> Theodosius</a>. The formation of a new province, called <a href="/wiki/Valentia_(Roman_Britain)" title="Valentia (Roman Britain)">Valentia</a> after the reigning emperor <a href="/wiki/Valens" title="Valens">Valens</a> (<span style="white-space:nowrap;"><abbr title="reigned">r.</abbr>&#160;364–378</span>), which may have been in Scotland, resulted.<sup id="cite_ref-:8_43-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:8-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> Roman military government was withdrawn from the island altogether by the early 5th century, resulting in the <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_settlement_of_Britain" title="Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain">Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain</a> and the immigration of the <a href="/wiki/Saxons" title="Saxons">Saxons</a> to southern Scotland and the rest of eastern Great Britain.<sup id="cite_ref-:8_43-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:8-43">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Middle_Ages">Middle Ages</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Early_Middle_Ages" title="Scotland in the Early Middle Ages">Scotland in the Early Middle Ages</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scotland_in_the_High_Middle_Ages" title="Scotland in the High Middle Ages">Scotland in the High Middle Ages</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Late_Middle_Ages" title="Scotland in the Late Middle Ages">Scotland in the Late Middle Ages</a></div>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti">.mw-parser-output .tmulti .multiimageinner{display:flex;flex-direction:column}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .theader{clear:both;font-weight:bold;text-align:center;align-self:center;background-color:transparent;width:100%}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .thumbcaption{background-color:transparent}.mw-parser-output .thumbcaption{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .tmulti .trow>.thumbcaption{text-align:center}}</style><div class="thumb tmulti tleft"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:392px;max-width:392px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:166px;max-width:166px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:231px;overflow:hidden"><a href="/wiki/File:Early_Medieval_Scotland_areas.png" class="image"><img alt="" class="thumbcaption">Political divisions in early medieval Scotland</div></div><div class="tsingle" style="width:222px;max-width:222px"><div class="thumbimage" style="height:231px;overflow:hidden"><a href="/wiki/File:Kingdom_of_Mann_and_the_Isles-en.svg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Kingdom_of_Mann_and_the_Isles-en.svg/220px-Kingdom_of_Mann_and_the_Isles-en.svg.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="231" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Kingdom_of_Mann_and_the_Isles-en.svg/330px-Kingdom_of_Mann_and_the_Isles-en.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Kingdom_of_Mann_and_the_Isles-en.svg/440px-Kingdom_of_Mann_and_the_Isles-en.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1297" data-file-height="1362" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption">Norse kingdoms at the end of the eleventh century</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>Beginning in the sixth century, the area that is now Scotland was divided into three areas: <a href="/wiki/Pictland" class="mw-redirect" title="Pictland">Pictland</a>, a patchwork of small lordships in central Scotland;<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 25–26">&#58;&#8202;25–26&#8202;</span></sup> the <a href="/wiki/Anglo-Saxon" class="mw-redirect" title="Anglo-Saxon">Anglo-Saxon</a> <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Northumbria" class="mw-redirect" title="Kingdom of Northumbria">Kingdom of Northumbria</a>, which had conquered southeastern Scotland;<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 18–20">&#58;&#8202;18–20&#8202;</span></sup> and <a href="/wiki/D%C3%A1l_Riata" title="Dál Riata">Dál Riata</a>, founded by settlers from Ireland, bringing Gaelic language and culture with them.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 20">&#58;&#8202;20&#8202;</span></sup> These societies were based on the family unit and had sharp divisions in wealth, although the vast majority were poor and worked full-time in <a href="/wiki/Subsistence_agriculture" title="Subsistence agriculture">subsistence agriculture</a>. The Picts kept slaves (mostly captured in war) through the ninth century.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 26–27">&#58;&#8202;26–27&#8202;</span></sup>
</p><p>Gaelic influence over Pictland and Northumbria was facilitated by the large number of <a href="/wiki/Celtic_Church" class="mw-redirect" title="Celtic Church">Gaelic-speaking clerics</a> working as missionaries.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-10" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 23–24">&#58;&#8202;23–24&#8202;</span></sup> Operating in the sixth century on the island of <a href="/wiki/Iona" title="Iona">Iona</a>, <a href="/wiki/Saint_Columba" class="mw-redirect" title="Saint Columba">Saint Columba</a> was one of the earliest and best-known missionaries.<sup id="cite_ref-short_40-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-short-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 39">&#58;&#8202;39&#8202;</span></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Vikings" title="Vikings">Vikings</a> began to raid Scotland in the eighth century. Although the raiders sought slaves and luxury items, their main motivation was to acquire land. The oldest <a href="/wiki/Norse_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Norse Scotland">Norse</a> settlements were in northwest Scotland, but they eventually conquered many areas along the coast. <a href="/wiki/Old_Norse" title="Old Norse">Old Norse</a> entirely displaced Gaelic in the <a href="/wiki/Northern_Isles" title="Northern Isles">Northern Isles</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 29–30">&#58;&#8202;29–30&#8202;</span></sup>
</p><p>In the ninth century, the Norse threat allowed a Gael named <a href="/wiki/Kenneth_I_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Kenneth I of Scotland">Cináed mac Ailpín</a> (Kenneth I) to seize power over Pictland, establishing a royal dynasty to which the modern monarchs trace their lineage, and marking the beginning of the end of Pictish culture.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 31–32">&#58;&#8202;31–32&#8202;</span></sup><sup id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup> The kingdom of Cináed and his descendants, called Alba, was Gaelic in character but existed on the same area as Pictland. By the end of the tenth century, the <a href="/wiki/Pictish_language" title="Pictish language">Pictish language</a> went extinct as its speakers shifted to Gaelic.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 32–33">&#58;&#8202;32–33&#8202;</span></sup> From a base in eastern Scotland north of the <a href="/wiki/River_Forth" title="River Forth">River Forth</a> and south of the <a href="/wiki/River_Spey" title="River Spey">River Spey</a>, the kingdom expanded first southwards, into the former Northumbrian lands, and northwards into <a href="/wiki/Province_of_Moray" title="Province of Moray">Moray</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 34–35">&#58;&#8202;34–35&#8202;</span></sup> Around the turn of the millennium, there was a centralization in agricultural lands and the first towns began to be established.<sup id="cite_ref-Forsyth_38-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Forsyth-38">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 36–37">&#58;&#8202;36–37&#8202;</span></sup>
</p><p>In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, much of Scotland was under the control of a single ruler. Initially, Gaelic culture predominated, but immigrants from France, England and Flanders steadily created a more diverse society, with the Gaelic language starting to be replaced by Scots. Altogether, a modern nation-state emerged from this. At the end of this period, war against England started the growth of a <a href="/wiki/Scottish_nationalism" title="Scottish nationalism">Scottish national consciousness</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Stringer_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stringer-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 37-39">&#58;&#8202;37-39&#8202;</span></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Barrell_2000_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Barrell_2000-48">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Location: ch 1">&#58;&#8202;ch 1&#8202;</span></sup> <a href="/wiki/David_I_of_Scotland" title="David I of Scotland">David I</a> (1124–1153) and his successors centralized royal power<sup id="cite_ref-Stringer_47-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stringer-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 41–42">&#58;&#8202;41–42&#8202;</span></sup> and united mainland Scotland, capturing regions such as Moray, <a href="/wiki/Galloway" title="Galloway">Galloway</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Caithness" title="Caithness">Caithness</a>, although he did not succeed at extending his power over the <a href="/wiki/Hebrides" title="Hebrides">Hebrides</a>, which had been ruled by various <a href="/wiki/Scottish_clans" class="mw-redirect" title="Scottish clans">Scottish clans</a> following the death of <a href="/wiki/Somerled" title="Somerled">Somerled</a> in 1164.<sup id="cite_ref-Stringer_47-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stringer-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 48–49">&#58;&#8202;48–49&#8202;</span></sup> The system of <a href="/wiki/Feudalism" title="Feudalism">feudalism</a> was consolidated, with both Anglo-Norman incomers and native Gaelic chieftains being granted land in exchange for serving the king.<sup id="cite_ref-Stringer_47-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stringer-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 53–54">&#58;&#8202;53–54&#8202;</span></sup> The complex relationship with Scotland's southern neighbour over this period is characterised by Scottish kings making successful and unsuccessful attempts to exploit English political turmoil, followed by the longest period of peace between Scotland and England in the mediaeval period: from 1217–1296.<sup id="cite_ref-Stringer_47-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stringer-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page: 45-46">&#58;&#8202;45-46&#8202;</span></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:252px;"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial,_Stirling.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial%2C_Stirling.jpg/250px-The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial%2C_Stirling.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="132" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial%2C_Stirling.jpg/375px-The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial%2C_Stirling.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial%2C_Stirling.jpg/500px-The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial%2C_Stirling.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4030" data-file-height="2129" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Wallace_Monument_Aerial,_Stirling.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/Wallace_Monument" title="Wallace Monument">Wallace Monument</a> commemorates <a href="/wiki/William_Wallace" title="William Wallace">William Wallace</a>, the 13th-century Scottish hero.</div></div></div>
<p>The death of <a href="/wiki/Alexander_III_of_Scotland" title="Alexander III of Scotland">Alexander III</a> in March 1286 broke the succession line of Scotland's kings. <a href="/wiki/Edward_I_of_England" title="Edward I of England">Edward I of England</a> arbitrated between various claimants for the Scottish crown. In return for surrendering Scotland's nominal independence, <a href="/wiki/John_Balliol" title="John Balliol">John Balliol</a> was pronounced king in 1292.<sup id="cite_ref-Stringer_47-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stringer-47">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 47">&#58;&#8202;47&#8202;</span></sup><sup id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> In 1294, Balliol and other Scottish lords refused Edward's demands to serve in his army against the French. Scotland and France sealed a treaty on 23 October 1295, known as the <a href="/wiki/Auld_Alliance" title="Auld Alliance">Auld Alliance</a>. War ensued, and John was deposed by Edward who took personal control of Scotland. <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Moray" title="Andrew Moray">Andrew Moray</a> and <a href="/wiki/William_Wallace" title="William Wallace">William Wallace</a> initially emerged as the principal leaders of the resistance to English rule in the <a href="/wiki/Wars_of_Scottish_Independence" title="Wars of Scottish Independence">Wars of Scottish Independence</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup> until <a href="/wiki/Robert_the_Bruce" title="Robert the Bruce">Robert the Bruce</a> was crowned king of Scotland in 1306.<sup id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup> Victory at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Bannockburn" title="Battle of Bannockburn">Battle of Bannockburn</a> in 1314 proved the Scots had regained control of their kingdom. In 1320 the world's first documented declaration of independence, the <a href="/wiki/Declaration_of_Arbroath" title="Declaration of Arbroath">Declaration of Arbroath</a>, won the support of <a href="/wiki/Pope_John_XXII" title="Pope John XXII">Pope John XXII</a>, leading to the legal recognition of Scottish sovereignty by the English Crown.
<sup id="cite_ref-Brown_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brown-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 70, 72">&#58;&#8202;70,&#8202;72&#8202;</span></sup>
</p><p>A civil war between the <a href="/wiki/Bruce_dynasty" class="mw-redirect" title="Bruce dynasty">Bruce dynasty</a> and their long-term rivals of the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Comyn" class="mw-redirect" title="House of Comyn">House of Comyn</a> and <a href="/wiki/House_of_Balliol" title="House of Balliol">House of Balliol</a> lasted until the middle of the 14th century. Although the Bruce faction was successful, <a href="/wiki/David_II_of_Scotland" title="David II of Scotland">David II's</a> lack of an heir allowed his half-nephew <a href="/wiki/Robert_II_of_Scotland" title="Robert II of Scotland">Robert II</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Lord_High_Steward_of_Scotland" title="Lord High Steward of Scotland">Lord High Steward of Scotland</a>, to come to the throne and establish the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Stewart" class="mw-redirect" title="House of Stewart">House of Stewart</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Brown_52-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brown-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 77">&#58;&#8202;77&#8202;</span></sup> The Stewarts ruled Scotland for the remainder of the <a href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</a>. The country they ruled experienced greater prosperity from the end of the 14th century through the Scottish Renaissance to the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Reformation" title="Scottish Reformation">Reformation</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-Mason_53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mason-53">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 93">&#58;&#8202;93&#8202;</span></sup> despite the effects of the <a href="/wiki/Black_Death" title="Black Death">Black Death</a> in 1349<sup id="cite_ref-Brown_52-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brown-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 76">&#58;&#8202;76&#8202;</span></sup> and increasing division between <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Highlands" title="Scottish Highlands">Highlands</a> and <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Lowlands" title="Scottish Lowlands">Lowlands</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Brown_52-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brown-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 78">&#58;&#8202;78&#8202;</span></sup> Multiple truces reduced warfare on the southern border.<sup id="cite_ref-Brown_52-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Brown-52">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 76, 83">&#58;&#8202;76,&#8202;83&#8202;</span></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_modern_period">Early modern period</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Scotland_in_the_early_modern_period" title="Scotland in the early modern period">Scotland in the early modern period</a></div>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="16th_century">16th century</span></h4>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_(1618-1620).jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_%281618-1620%29.jpg/170px-Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_%281618-1620%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="282" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_%281618-1620%29.jpg/255px-Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_%281618-1620%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_%281618-1620%29.jpg/340px-Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_%281618-1620%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="3394" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Portrait_of_King_James_I_%26_VI_(1618-1620).jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/James_VI_and_I" title="James VI and I">James VI</a> succeeded to the English and Irish thrones in 1603.</div></div></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Perpetual_Peace" title="Treaty of Perpetual Peace">Treaty of Perpetual Peace</a> was signed in 1502 by <a href="/wiki/James_IV_of_Scotland" title="James IV of Scotland">James IV of Scotland</a> and <a href="/wiki/Henry_VII_of_England" title="Henry VII of England">Henry VII of England</a>. James married Henry's daughter, <a href="/wiki/Margaret_Tudor" title="Margaret Tudor">Margaret Tudor</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> James invaded England in support of France under the terms of the Auld Alliance and became the last British monarch to die in battle, at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Flodden" title="Battle of Flodden">Flodden</a> in 1513.<sup id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup> In 1560, the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Edinburgh" title="Treaty of Edinburgh">Treaty of Edinburgh</a> brought an end to the Anglo-French conflict and recognized the Protestant <a href="/wiki/Elizabeth_I" title="Elizabeth I">Elizabeth I</a> as Queen of England.<sup id="cite_ref-Mason_53-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mason-53">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 112">&#58;&#8202;112&#8202;</span></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland" title="Parliament of Scotland">Parliament of Scotland</a> met and immediately adopted the <a href="/wiki/Scots_Confession" title="Scots Confession">Scots Confession</a>, which signalled the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Reformation" title="Scottish Reformation">Scottish Reformation</a>'s sharp break from papal authority and Roman Catholic teaching.<sup id="cite_ref-short_40-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-short-40">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 44">&#58;&#8202;44&#8202;</span></sup> The Catholic <a href="/wiki/Mary,_Queen_of_Scots" title="Mary, Queen of Scots">Mary, Queen of Scots</a> was forced to abdicate in 1567.<sup id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="17th_century">17th century</span></h4>
<p>In 1603, <a href="/wiki/James_VI_and_I" title="James VI and I">James VI, King of Scots</a> inherited the thrones of the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_England" title="Kingdom of England">Kingdom of England</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Ireland" title="Kingdom of Ireland">Kingdom of Ireland</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Union_of_the_Crowns" title="Union of the Crowns">Union of the Crowns</a>, and moved to London.<sup id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> The first <a href="/wiki/Union_Jack" title="Union Jack">Union Jack</a> was designed at James's behest, to be flown in addition to the <a href="/wiki/Flag_of_Scotland" title="Flag of Scotland">St Andrew's Cross</a> on Scots vessels at sea. James VI and I intended to create a single kingdom of Great Britain, but was thwarted in his attempt to do so by the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_England" title="Parliament of England">Parliament of England</a>, which supported the wrecking proposal that a full legal union be sought instead, a proposal to which the Scots Parliament would not assent, causing the king to withdraw the plan.<sup id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>With the exception of a short period under <a href="/wiki/The_Protectorate" title="The Protectorate">the Protectorate</a>, Scotland remained a separate state in the 17th century, but there was considerable conflict between the crown and the <a href="/wiki/Covenanters" title="Covenanters">Covenanters</a> over the form of <a href="/wiki/Presbyterian_church_governance" class="mw-redirect" title="Presbyterian church governance">church government</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Wormald_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wormald-59">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 124">&#58;&#8202;124&#8202;</span></sup> The military was strengthened, allowing the imposition of royal authority on the western Highland clans. The 1609 <a href="/wiki/Statutes_of_Iona" title="Statutes of Iona">Statutes of Iona</a> compelled the cultural integration of Hebridean clan leaders.<sup id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 37–40">&#58;&#8202;37–40&#8202;</span></sup> In 1641 and again in 1643, the Parliament of Scotland unsuccessfully sought a union with England which was "federative" and not "incorporating", in which Scotland would retain a separate parliament.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> The issue of union split the parliament in 1648.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the execution of the Scottish king at <a href="/wiki/Whitehall" title="Whitehall">Whitehall</a> in 1649, amid the <a href="/wiki/Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms" title="Wars of the Three Kingdoms">Wars of the Three Kingdoms</a> and <a href="/wiki/Scotland_in_the_Wars_of_the_Three_Kingdoms" title="Scotland in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms">its events in Scotland</a>, <a href="/wiki/Oliver_Cromwell" title="Oliver Cromwell">Oliver Cromwell</a>, the victorious <a href="/wiki/Lord_Protector" title="Lord Protector">Lord Protector</a>, imposed the British Isles' first written constitution – the <a href="/wiki/Instrument_of_Government" title="Instrument of Government">Instrument of Government</a> – on Scotland in 1652 as part of the republican <a href="/wiki/Commonwealth_of_England,_Scotland,_and_Ireland" class="mw-redirect" title="Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland">Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> The Protectorate Parliament was the first Westminster parliament to include representatives nominally from Scotland. The monarchy of the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Stuart" title="House of Stuart">House of Stuart</a> was resumed with the <a href="/wiki/Restoration_in_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Restoration in Scotland">Restoration in Scotland</a> in 1660.
</p><p>The Parliament of Scotland sought a commercial union with England in 1664; the proposal was rejected in 1668.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> In 1670 the Parliament of England rejected a proposed political union with Scotland.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> English proposals along the same lines were abandoned in 1674 and in 1685.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Altimarlach" title="Battle of Altimarlach">Battle of Altimarlach</a> in 1680 was the last significant clan battle fought between <a href="/wiki/Scottish_clan" title="Scottish clan">highland clans</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup> After the fall and flight into exile of the Catholic Stuart king, <a href="/wiki/James_VII_and_II" class="mw-redirect" title="James VII and II">James VII and II</a> the <a href="/wiki/Glorious_Revolution_in_Scotland" title="Glorious Revolution in Scotland">Glorious Revolution in Scotland</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Convention_of_Estates_(1689)" title="Convention of Estates (1689)">Convention of Estates</a> replaced the House of Stuart in favour of <a href="/wiki/William_III_of_England" title="William III of England">William III</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mary_II_of_England" title="Mary II of England">Mary II</a> who was Mary Stuart.<sup id="cite_ref-Wormald_59-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Wormald-59">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 142">&#58;&#8202;142&#8202;</span></sup> The Scots Parliament rejected proposals for a political union in 1689.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Jacobitism" title="Jacobitism">Jacobitism</a>, the political support for the exiled Catholic Stuart dynasty, remained a threat to the security of the British state under the Protestant <a href="/wiki/House_of_Orange" class="mw-redirect" title="House of Orange">House of Orange</a> and the succeeding <a href="/wiki/House_of_Hanover" title="House of Hanover">House of Hanover</a> until the defeat of the <a href="/wiki/Jacobite_rising_of_1745" title="Jacobite rising of 1745">Jacobite rising of 1745</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In common with countries such as France, Norway, Sweden and Finland, Scotland experienced <a href="/wiki/Seven_ill_years" title="Seven ill years">famines</a> during the 1690s. Mortality, reduced childbirths and increased emigration reduced the population of parts of the country about 10–15%.<sup id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup> In 1698, the <a href="/wiki/Company_of_Scotland" title="Company of Scotland">Company of Scotland</a> attempted a project to secure a trading colony on the <a href="/wiki/Isthmus_of_Panama" title="Isthmus of Panama">Isthmus of Panama</a>. Almost every Scottish landowner who had money to spare is said to have invested in the <a href="/wiki/Darien_scheme" title="Darien scheme">Darien scheme</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-:6_64-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:6-64">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:7_65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:7-65">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After another proposal from the English House of Lords was rejected in 1695, and a further Lords motion was voted down in the House of Commons in 1700, the Parliament of Scotland again rejected union in 1702.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-8" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup> The failure of the Darien Scheme bankrupted the landowners who had invested, though not the burghs. Nevertheless, the nobles' bankruptcy, along with the threat of an English invasion, played a leading role in convincing the Scots elite to back a union with England.<sup id="cite_ref-:6_64-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:6-64">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:7_65-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:7-65">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup> On 22 July 1706, the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Union" title="Treaty of Union">Treaty of Union</a> was agreed between representatives of the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Scotland" title="Parliament of Scotland">Scots Parliament</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_England" title="Parliament of England">Parliament of England</a>. The following year, twin <a href="/wiki/Acts_of_Union_1707" title="Acts of Union 1707">Acts of Union</a> were passed by both parliaments to create the united <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain" title="Kingdom of Great Britain">Kingdom of Great Britain</a> with effect from 1 May 1707<sup id="cite_ref-Mackie_24-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mackie-24">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup> with popular opposition and anti-union riots in <a href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</a>, <a href="/wiki/Glasgow" title="Glasgow">Glasgow</a>, and elsewhere.<sup id="cite_ref-1707_protests_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-1707_protests-66">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup> The newly formed <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Great_Britain" title="Parliament of Great Britain">Parliament of Great Britain</a> rejected proposals from the <a href="/wiki/Parliament_of_Ireland" title="Parliament of Ireland">Parliament of Ireland</a> that the third kingdom be incorporated in the union.<sup id="cite_ref-:5_61-9" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:5-61">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="18th_century">18th century</span></h4>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg/220px-The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="133" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg/330px-The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d5/The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg/440px-The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2000" data-file-height="1207" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Battle_of_Culloden.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/David_Morier" title="David Morier">David Morier</a>'s depiction of the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Culloden" title="Battle of Culloden">Battle of Culloden</a> - <i><a href="/wiki/An_Incident_in_the_Rebellion_of_1745" title="An Incident in the Rebellion of 1745">An Incident in the Rebellion of 1745</a></i></div></div></div>
<p>With trade tariffs with England abolished, trade blossomed, especially with <a href="/wiki/Colonial_America" class="mw-redirect" title="Colonial America">Colonial America</a>. The clippers belonging to the Glasgow <a href="/wiki/Tobacco_Lords" title="Tobacco Lords">Tobacco Lords</a> were the fastest ships on the route to <a href="/wiki/Virginia" title="Virginia">Virginia</a>. Until the <a href="/wiki/American_War_of_Independence" class="mw-redirect" title="American War of Independence">American War of Independence</a> in 1776, Glasgow was the world's premier tobacco port, dominating world trade.<sup id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-68">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> The disparity between the wealth of the merchant classes of the Scottish Lowlands and the ancient clans of the Scottish Highlands grew, amplifying centuries of division.
</p><p>The deposed <a href="/wiki/Jacobitism" title="Jacobitism">Jacobite Stuart</a> claimants had remained popular in the Highlands and north-east, particularly amongst non-<a href="/wiki/Presbyterian" class="mw-redirect" title="Presbyterian">Presbyterians</a>, including Roman Catholics and <a href="/wiki/Episcopalian_Protestants" class="mw-redirect" title="Episcopalian Protestants">Episcopalian Protestants</a>. Two major Jacobite risings launched in <a href="/wiki/Jacobite_rising_of_1715" title="Jacobite rising of 1715">1715</a> and <a href="/wiki/Jacobite_rising_of_1745" title="Jacobite rising of 1745">1745</a> failed to remove the <a href="/wiki/House_of_Hanover" title="House of Hanover">House of Hanover</a> from the British throne. The threat of the Jacobite movement to the United Kingdom and its monarchs effectively ended at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Culloden" title="Battle of Culloden">Battle of Culloden</a>, Great Britain's last <a href="/wiki/Pitched_battle" title="Pitched battle">pitched battle</a>.
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Enlightenment" title="Scottish Enlightenment">Scottish Enlightenment</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</a> turned Scotland into an intellectual, commercial and industrial powerhouse<sup id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-69">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> — so much so <a href="/wiki/Voltaire" title="Voltaire">Voltaire</a> said "We look to Scotland for all our ideas of civilisation."<sup id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-70">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> With the demise of Jacobitism and the advent of the Union, thousands of Scots, mainly Lowlanders, took up numerous positions of power in politics, civil service, the army and navy, trade, economics, colonial enterprises and other areas across the nascent <a href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British Empire</a>. Historian Neil Davidson notes "after 1746 there was an entirely new level of participation by Scots in political life, particularly outside Scotland." Davidson also states "far from being 'peripheral' to the British economy, Scotland – or more precisely, the Lowlands – lay at its core."<sup id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-71">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the Highlands, clan chiefs gradually started to think of themselves more as commercial landlords than leaders of their people. These social and economic changes included the first phase of the <a href="/wiki/Highland_Clearances" title="Highland Clearances">Highland Clearances</a> and, ultimately, the demise of clanship.<sup id="cite_ref-Devine_1994_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Devine_1994-72">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap"><span title="Page / location: 32–53, passim">&#58;&#8202;32–53,&#8202;<i>passim</i>&#8202;</span></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="19th_century">19th century</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Scotland_in_the_modern_era" title="Scotland in the modern era">Scotland in the modern era</a></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg/220px-Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="128" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg/330px-Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg/440px-Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3584" data-file-height="2081" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Tourists_posing_at_the_National_Monument_of_Scotland.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/National_Monument_of_Scotland" title="National Monument of Scotland">National Monument of Scotland</a> on <a href="/wiki/Calton_Hill" title="Calton Hill">Calton Hill</a> in Edinburgh is the national memorial to Scottish soldiers lost in the <a href="/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars" title="Napoleonic Wars">Napoleonic Wars</a>.</div></div></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Reform_Act_1832" title="Scottish Reform Act 1832">Scottish Reform Act 1832</a> increased the number of Scottish MPs and widened the franchise to include more of the middle classes.<sup id="cite_ref-Devine&amp;Finlay1996pp64-5_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Devine&amp;Finlay1996pp64-5-73">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> From the mid-century, there were increasing calls for Home Rule for Scotland and the post of <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Scotland" title="Secretary of State for Scotland">Secretary of State for Scotland</a> was revived.<sup id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-74">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> Towards the end of the century Prime Ministers of Scottish descent included <a href="/wiki/William_Ewart_Gladstone" title="William Ewart Gladstone">William Gladstone</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-Quinault2007_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Quinault2007-75">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Archibald_Primrose,_5th_Earl_of_Rosebery" title="Archibald Primrose, 5th Earl of Rosebery">the Earl of Rosebery</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-76">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup> In the late 19th century the growing importance of the working classes was marked by <a href="/wiki/Keir_Hardie" title="Keir Hardie">Keir Hardie</a>'s success in the <a href="/wiki/Mid_Lanarkshire_by-election,_1888" class="mw-redirect" title="Mid Lanarkshire by-election, 1888">Mid Lanarkshire by-election, 1888</a>, leading to the foundation of the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Labour_Party_(1888)" title="Scottish Labour Party (1888)">Scottish Labour Party</a>, which was absorbed into the <a href="/wiki/Independent_Labour_Party" title="Independent Labour Party">Independent Labour Party</a> in 1895, with Hardie as its first leader.<sup id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-77">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Glasgow became one of the largest cities in the world and known as "the <a href="/wiki/Second_City_of_the_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Second City of the Empire">Second City of the Empire</a>" after London.<sup id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-78">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup> After 1860, the Clydeside shipyards specialised in steamships made of iron (after 1870, made of steel), which rapidly replaced the wooden sailing vessels of both the merchant fleets and the battle fleets of the world. It became the world's pre-eminent shipbuilding centre.<sup id="cite_ref-Shields1949_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Shields1949-79">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> The industrial developments, while they brought work and wealth, were so rapid that housing, town-planning, and provision for public health did not keep pace with them, and for a time living conditions in some of the towns and cities were notoriously bad, with overcrowding, high infant mortality, and growing rates of tuberculosis.<sup id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-80">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg/170px-Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="206" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg/255px-Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg/340px-Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1649" data-file-height="2000" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Portrait_of_Sir_Walter_Scott.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Walter_Scott" title="Walter Scott">Walter Scott</a>, whose <a href="/wiki/Waverley_Novels" title="Waverley Novels">Waverley Novels</a> helped define Scottish identity in the 19th century</div></div></div>
<p>While the Scottish Enlightenment is traditionally considered to have concluded toward the end of the 18th century,<sup id="cite_ref-Magnusson_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Magnusson-81">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> disproportionately large Scottish contributions to British science and letters continued for another 50 years or more, thanks to such figures as the physicists <a href="/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell" title="James Clerk Maxwell">James Clerk Maxwell</a> and <a href="/wiki/William_Thomson,_1st_Baron_Kelvin" title="William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin">Lord Kelvin</a>, and the engineers and inventors <a href="/wiki/James_Watt" title="James Watt">James Watt</a> and <a href="/wiki/William_Murdoch" title="William Murdoch">William Murdoch</a>, whose work was critical to the technological developments of the Industrial Revolution throughout Britain.<sup id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-82">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup> In literature, the most successful figure of the mid-19th century was <a href="/wiki/Walter_Scott" title="Walter Scott">Walter Scott</a>. His first prose work, <i><a href="/wiki/Waverley_(novel)" title="Waverley (novel)">Waverley</a></i> in 1814, is often called the first historical novel.<sup id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-83">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> It launched a highly successful career that probably more than any other helped define and popularise Scottish cultural identity.<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> In the late 19th century, a number of Scottish-born authors achieved international reputations, such as <a href="/wiki/Robert_Louis_Stevenson" title="Robert Louis Stevenson">Robert Louis Stevenson</a>, <a href="/wiki/Arthur_Conan_Doyle" title="Arthur Conan Doyle">Arthur Conan Doyle</a>, <a href="/wiki/J._M._Barrie" title="J. M. Barrie">J. M. Barrie</a> and <a href="/wiki/George_MacDonald" title="George MacDonald">George MacDonald</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-85">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup> Scotland also played a major part in the development of art and architecture. The <a href="/wiki/Glasgow_School" title="Glasgow School">Glasgow School</a>, which developed in the late 19th century, and flourished in the early 20th century, produced a distinctive blend of influences including the <a href="/wiki/Celtic_Revival" title="Celtic Revival">Celtic Revival</a> the <a href="/wiki/Arts_and_Crafts_movement" title="Arts and Crafts movement">Arts and Crafts movement</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Japonism" class="mw-redirect" title="Japonism">Japonism</a>, which found favour throughout the <a href="/wiki/Modern_art" title="Modern art">modern art</a> world of continental Europe and helped define the <a href="/wiki/Art_Nouveau" title="Art Nouveau">Art Nouveau</a> style. Proponents included architect and artist <a href="/wiki/Charles_Rennie_Mackintosh" title="Charles Rennie Mackintosh">Charles Rennie Mackintosh</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-86">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>This period saw a process of rehabilitation for Highland culture. In the 1820s, as part of the <a href="/wiki/Romanticism" title="Romanticism">Romantic revival</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tartan" title="Tartan">tartan</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Kilt" title="Kilt">kilt</a> were adopted by members of the social elite, not just in Scotland, but across Europe,<sup id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-87">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Sievers2007_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Sievers2007-88">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> prompted by the popularity of Macpherson's <a href="/wiki/Ossian" title="Ossian">Ossian</a> cycle<sup id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-89">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-90">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup> and then Walter Scott's Waverley novels.<sup id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-91">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> The Highlands remained poor and the only part of mainland Britain with a recurrent famine. A small range of products were exported from the region, which had negligible industrial production and a continued population growth that tested the subsistence agriculture. These problems, and the desire to improve agriculture and profits were the driving forces of the ongoing <a href="/wiki/Highland_Clearances" title="Highland Clearances">Highland Clearances</a>, in which many of the population of the Highlands suffered eviction as lands were enclosed, principally so that they could be used for sheep farming. The first phase of the clearances followed patterns of agricultural change throughout Britain. The second phase was driven by overpopulation, the <a href="/wiki/Highland_Potato_Famine" title="Highland Potato Famine">Highland Potato Famine</a> and the collapse of industries that had relied on the wartime economy of the Napoleonic Wars.<sup id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-92">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> The population of Scotland grew steadily in the 19th century, from 1,608,000 in the census of 1801 to 2,889,000 in 1851 and 4,472,000 in 1901.<sup id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-93">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup> Even with the development of industry, there were not enough good jobs. As a result, during the period 1841–1931, about 2 million Scots migrated to North America and Australia, and another 750,000 Scots relocated to England.<sup id="cite_ref-Huston&amp;Knox2001pxxxii_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Huston&amp;Knox2001pxxxii-94">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:352px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg/350px-Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg" decoding="async" width="350" height="157" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg/525px-Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg/700px-Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2400" data-file-height="1079" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Disruption_forming_Free_Kirk.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The Disruption Assembly; painted by <a href="/wiki/David_Octavius_Hill" title="David Octavius Hill">David Octavius Hill</a></div></div></div>
<p>After prolonged years of struggle in the Kirk, the Evangelicals gained control of the <a href="/wiki/General_Assembly_of_the_Church_of_Scotland" title="General Assembly of the Church of Scotland">General Assembly</a> in 1834 and passed the Veto Act, which allowed congregations to reject unwanted "intrusive" presentations to livings by patrons. The following "Ten Years' Conflict" of legal and political wrangling ended in defeat for the non-intrusionists in the civil courts. The result was a schism from the church by some of the non-intrusionists led by Dr <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Chalmers" title="Thomas Chalmers">Thomas Chalmers</a>, known as the Great <a href="/wiki/Disruption_of_1843" title="Disruption of 1843">Disruption of 1843</a>. Roughly a third of the clergy, mainly from the North and Highlands, formed the separate <a href="/wiki/Free_Church_of_Scotland_(1843%E2%80%931900)" title="Free Church of Scotland (1843–1900)">Free Church of Scotland</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Robb1990_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Robb1990-95">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> In the late 19th century growing divisions between fundamentalist Calvinists and theological liberals resulted in a further split in the Free Church as the rigid Calvinists broke away to form the <a href="/wiki/Free_Presbyterian_Church_of_Scotland" title="Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland">Free Presbyterian Church</a> in 1893.<sup id="cite_ref-Koch2006p416-7_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Koch2006p416-7-96">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Catholic_emancipation" title="Catholic emancipation">Catholic emancipation</a> in 1829 and the influx of large numbers of Irish immigrants, particularly after the famine years of the late 1840s, mainly to the growing lowland centres like Glasgow, led to a transformation in the fortunes of Catholicism. In 1878, despite opposition, a Roman Catholic ecclesiastical hierarchy was restored to the country, and Catholicism became a significant denomination within Scotland.<sup id="cite_ref-Koch2006p416-7_96-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Koch2006p416-7-96">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Industrialisation, urbanisation and the Disruption of 1843 all undermined the tradition of parish schools. From 1830 the state began to fund buildings with grants; then from 1846 it was funding schools by direct sponsorship; and in 1872 Scotland moved to a system like that in England of state-sponsored largely free schools, run by local school boards.<sup id="cite_ref-Devine2001p91-100_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Devine2001p91-100-97">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup> The historic <a href="/wiki/University_of_Glasgow" title="University of Glasgow">University of Glasgow</a> became a leader in British higher education by providing the educational needs of youth from the urban and commercial classes, as opposed to the upper class.<sup id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-98">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/The_University_of_St_Andrews" class="mw-redirect" title="The University of St Andrews">The University of St Andrews</a> pioneered the admission of women to Scottish universities.
