From 1892 Scottish universities could admit and graduate women and the numbers of women at Scottish universities steadily increased until the early 20th century.<sup id="cite_ref-Rayner-Canham2008_99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Rayner-Canham2008-99">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:-Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/-Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg/220px--Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="178" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/-Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg/330px--Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/-Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg/440px--Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2511" data-file-height="2026" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:-Spying_in_Glenfeshie-_MET_DP148525.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Deer stalkers on Glenfeshie Estate spying with <a href="/wiki/Monocular" title="Monocular">monoculars</a>, ca. 1858</div></div></div>
<p>Caused by the advent of <a href="/wiki/Refrigeration" title="Refrigeration">refrigeration</a> and imports of lamb, mutton and wool from overseas, the 1870s brought with them a collapse of sheep prices and an abrupt halt in the previous sheep farming boom.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_100-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> Land prices subsequently plummeted, too, and accelerated the process of the so-called "Balmoralisation" of Scotland, an era in the second half of the 19th century that saw an increase in tourism and the establishment of large estates dedicated to <a href="/wiki/Hunting" title="Hunting">field sports</a> like <a href="/wiki/Deer_stalking" title="Deer stalking">deer stalking</a> and <a href="/wiki/Driven_grouse_shooting" title="Driven grouse shooting">grouse shooting</a>, especially in the Scottish Highlands.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_100-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:1_101-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-101">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> The process was named after <a href="/wiki/Balmoral_estate" class="mw-redirect" title="Balmoral estate">Balmoral estate</a>, purchased by Queen Victoria in 1848, that fuelled the romanticisation of upland Scotland and initiated an influx of the newly wealthy acquiring similar estates in the following decades.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_100-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-:1_101-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:1-101">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> In the late 19th century just 118 people owned half of Scotland, with nearly 60 per cent of the whole country being part of shooting estates.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_100-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup> While their relative importance has somewhat declined due to changing recreational interests throughout the 20th century, deer stalking and grouse shooting remain of prime importance on many private estates in Scotland.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_100-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-100">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-102">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="20th_century">20th century</span></h3>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front,_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front%2C_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg/220px-The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front%2C_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="179" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front%2C_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg/330px-The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front%2C_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front%2C_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg/440px-The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front%2C_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3045" data-file-height="2480" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Cooperation_of_the_Allied_Forces_on_the_Western_Front,_1914-1918_Q7179.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Douglas_Haig" class="mw-redirect" title="Douglas Haig">Douglas Haig</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ferdinand_Foch" title="Ferdinand Foch">Ferdinand Foch</a> inspecting the <a href="/wiki/Gordon_Highlanders" title="Gordon Highlanders">Gordon Highlanders</a>, 1918</div></div></div>
<p>Scotland played a major role in the <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_United_Kingdom_during_the_First_World_War" title="History of the United Kingdom during the First World War">British effort</a> in the <a href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</a>. It especially provided manpower, ships, machinery, fish and money.<sup id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-103">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup> With a population of 4.8 million in 1911, Scotland sent over half a million men to the war, of whom over a quarter died in combat or from disease, and 150,000 were seriously wounded.<sup id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-104">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Field_Marshal_(United_Kingdom)" class="mw-redirect" title="Field Marshal (United Kingdom)">Field Marshal</a> <a href="/wiki/Douglas_Haig" class="mw-redirect" title="Douglas Haig">Sir Douglas Haig</a> was Britain's commander on the Western Front.
</p><p>The war saw the emergence of a radical movement called "<a href="/wiki/Red_Clydeside" title="Red Clydeside">Red Clydeside</a>" led by militant trades unionists. Formerly a <a href="/wiki/Liberal_Party_(UK)" title="Liberal Party (UK)">Liberal</a> stronghold, the industrial districts switched to <a href="/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)" title="Labour Party (UK)">Labour</a> by 1922, with a base among the <a href="/wiki/Irish_Catholic" class="mw-redirect" title="Irish Catholic">Irish Catholic</a> working-class districts. Women were especially active in building neighbourhood solidarity on housing issues. The "Reds" operated within the Labour Party with little influence in Parliament and the mood changed to passive despair by the late 1920s.<sup id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-105">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The shipbuilding industry expanded by a third and expected renewed prosperity, but instead, a serious depression hit the economy by 1922 and it did not fully recover until 1939. The interwar years were marked by economic stagnation in rural and urban areas, and high unemployment.<sup id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-106">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> Indeed, the war brought with it deep social, cultural, economic, and political dislocations. Thoughtful Scots pondered their declension, as the main social indicators such as poor health, bad housing, and long-term mass unemployment, pointed to terminal social and economic stagnation at best, or even a downward spiral. Service abroad on behalf of the Empire lost its allure to ambitious young people, who left Scotland permanently. The heavy dependence on obsolescent heavy industry and mining was a central problem, and no one offered workable solutions. The despair reflected what Finlay (1994) describes as a widespread sense of hopelessness that prepared local business and political leaders to accept a new orthodoxy of centralised government economic planning when it arrived during the <a href="/wiki/Second_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Second World War">Second World War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-107">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During the Second World War, Scotland was targeted by <a href="/wiki/Nazi_Germany" title="Nazi Germany">Nazi Germany</a> largely due to its factories, shipyards, and coal mines.<sup id="cite_ref-blitz_108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-blitz-108">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> Cities such as <a href="/wiki/Glasgow" title="Glasgow">Glasgow</a> and <a href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</a> were targeted by German bombers, as were smaller towns mostly located in the central belt of the country.<sup id="cite_ref-blitz_108-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-blitz-108">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> Perhaps the most significant air-raid in Scotland was the <a href="/wiki/Clydebank_Blitz" title="Clydebank Blitz">Clydebank Blitz</a> of March 1941, which intended to destroy naval shipbuilding in the area.<sup id="cite_ref-Clydebank_blitz_109-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Clydebank_blitz-109">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup> 528 people were killed and 4,000 homes totally destroyed.<sup id="cite_ref-Clydebank_blitz_109-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Clydebank_blitz-109">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg/220px-Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="128" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg/330px-Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg/440px-Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg 2x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="292" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Rudolf_Hess_-_Bf_110D_Werk_Nr_3869_-_Wreckage_-_Bonnyton_Moor.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Rudolf_Hess" title="Rudolf Hess">Rudolf Hess</a>, <a href="/wiki/Deputy_F%C3%BChrer" class="mw-redirect" title="Deputy Führer">Deputy Führer of Nazi Germany</a>, crashed his plane at <a href="/wiki/Eaglesham" title="Eaglesham">Bonnyton Moor</a> in the Scottish central belt in an attempt to make peace.</div></div></div>
<p>Perhaps Scotland's most unusual wartime episode occurred in 1941 when <a href="/wiki/Rudolf_Hess" title="Rudolf Hess">Rudolf Hess</a> flew to Renfrewshire, possibly intending to broker a peace deal through the <a href="/wiki/Duke_of_Hamilton" title="Duke of Hamilton">Duke of Hamilton</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-110">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup> Before his departure from Germany, Hess had given his adjutant, <a href="/wiki/Karlheinz_Pintsch" title="Karlheinz Pintsch">Karlheinz Pintsch</a>, a letter addressed to Hitler that detailed his intentions to open peace negotiations with the British. Pintsch delivered the letter to Hitler at the Berghof around noon on 11 May.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEvans2008168_111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEvans2008168-111">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Albert_Speer" title="Albert Speer">Albert Speer</a> later said Hitler described Hess's departure as one of the worst personal blows of his life, as he considered it a personal betrayal.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESereny1996240_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESereny1996240-112">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> Hitler worried that his allies, Italy and Japan, would perceive Hess's act as an attempt by Hitler to secretly open peace negotiations with the British.
</p>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg/220px-Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="219" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg/330px-Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg/440px-Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg 2x" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="798" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Royal_Scots_with_flag_01-1945.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Royal_Scots" title="Royal Scots">Royal Scots</a> with a captured <a href="/wiki/Empire_of_Japan" title="Empire of Japan">Japanese</a> <a href="/wiki/Good_Luck_Flag" title="Good Luck Flag">Hinomaru Yosegaki</a> flag, <a href="/wiki/British_rule_in_Burma" title="British rule in Burma">Burma</a>, 1945</div></div></div>
<p>As in World War I, <a href="/wiki/Scapa_Flow" title="Scapa Flow">Scapa Flow</a> in Orkney served as an important <a href="/wiki/Royal_Navy" title="Royal Navy">Royal Navy</a> base. Attacks on Scapa Flow and <a href="/wiki/Rosyth" title="Rosyth">Rosyth</a> gave RAF fighters their first successes downing bombers in the <a href="/wiki/Firth_of_Forth" title="Firth of Forth">Firth of Forth</a> and <a href="/wiki/East_Lothian" title="East Lothian">East Lothian</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-113">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup> The shipyards and heavy engineering factories in <a href="/wiki/Glasgow" title="Glasgow">Glasgow</a> and Clydeside played a key part in the war effort, and suffered attacks from the <a href="/wiki/Luftwaffe" title="Luftwaffe">Luftwaffe</a>, enduring great destruction and loss of life.<sup id="cite_ref-Buchanan2003p51_114-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Buchanan2003p51-114">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> As transatlantic voyages involved negotiating north-west Britain, Scotland played a key part in the battle of the North Atlantic.<sup id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-115">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Shetland" title="Shetland">Shetland</a>'s relative proximity to occupied Norway resulted in the <a href="/wiki/Shetland_bus" title="Shetland bus">Shetland bus</a> by which fishing boats helped Norwegians flee the <a href="/wiki/Nazis" class="mw-redirect" title="Nazis">Nazis</a>, and expeditions across the <a href="/wiki/North_Sea" title="North Sea">North Sea</a> to assist resistance.<sup id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-116">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Scottish industry came out of the depression slump by a dramatic expansion of its industrial activity, absorbing unemployed men and many women as well. The shipyards were the centre of more activity, but many smaller industries produced the machinery needed by the British bombers, tanks and warships.<sup id="cite_ref-Buchanan2003p51_114-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Buchanan2003p51-114">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> Agriculture prospered, as did all sectors except for coal mining, which was operating mines near exhaustion. Real wages, adjusted for inflation, rose 25% and unemployment temporarily vanished. Increased income, and the more equal distribution of food, obtained through a tight rationing system, dramatically improved the health and nutrition.
</p>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament,_1999.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament%2C_1999.jpg/220px-Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament%2C_1999.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="156" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament%2C_1999.jpg/330px-Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament%2C_1999.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament%2C_1999.jpg/440px-Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament%2C_1999.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3508" data-file-height="2480" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Opening_of_the_Scottish_Parliament,_1999.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The official reconvening of the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament" title="Scottish Parliament">Scottish Parliament</a> in July 1999 with <a href="/wiki/Donald_Dewar" title="Donald Dewar">Donald Dewar</a>, then <a href="/wiki/First_minister_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="First minister of Scotland">first minister of Scotland</a> (left) with <a href="/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Queen Elizabeth II">Queen Elizabeth II</a> (centre) and <a href="/wiki/Presiding_Officer_of_the_Scottish_Parliament" title="Presiding Officer of the Scottish Parliament">Presiding Officer</a> <a href="/wiki/Sir_David_Steel" class="mw-redirect" title="Sir David Steel">Sir David Steel</a> (right)</div></div></div>
<p>After 1945, Scotland's economic situation worsened due to overseas competition, inefficient industry, and industrial disputes.<sup id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-117">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> Only in recent decades has the country enjoyed something of a cultural and economic renaissance. Economic factors contributing to this recovery included a resurgent financial services industry, <a href="/wiki/Electronics_manufacturing" class="mw-redirect" title="Electronics manufacturing">electronics manufacturing</a>, (see <a href="/wiki/Silicon_Glen" title="Silicon Glen">Silicon Glen</a>),<sup id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-118">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup> and the <a href="/wiki/North_Sea_oil" title="North Sea oil">North Sea oil</a> and gas industry.<sup id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-119">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup> The introduction in 1989 by Margaret Thatcher's government of the <a href="/wiki/Poll_tax_(Great_Britain)" title="Poll tax (Great Britain)">Community Charge</a> (widely known as the Poll Tax) one year before the rest of Great Britain,<sup id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-120">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup> contributed to a growing movement for Scottish control over domestic affairs.<sup id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-121">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup> Following a <a href="/wiki/Scottish_devolution_referendum,_1997" class="mw-redirect" title="Scottish devolution referendum, 1997">referendum on devolution proposals in 1997</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Scotland_Act_1998" title="Scotland Act 1998">Scotland Act 1998</a><sup id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-122">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup> was passed by the British Parliament, which established a devolved <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament" title="Scottish Parliament">Scottish Parliament</a> and <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Government" title="Scottish Government">Scottish Government</a> with responsibility for most laws specific to Scotland.<sup id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-123">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup> The Scottish Parliament was reconvened in <a href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</a> on 4 July 1999.<sup id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-124">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup> The first to hold the office of <a href="/wiki/First_minister_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="First minister of Scotland">first minister of Scotland</a> was <a href="/wiki/Donald_Dewar" title="Donald Dewar">Donald Dewar</a>, who served until his sudden death in 2000.<sup id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-125">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="21st_century">21st century</span></h3>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament_Building" title="Scottish Parliament Building">Scottish Parliament Building</a> at Holyrood opened in October 2004 after lengthy construction delays and running over budget.<sup id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-126">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup> The Scottish Parliament's form of <a href="/wiki/Proportional_representation" title="Proportional representation">proportional representation</a> (the <a href="/wiki/Additional_member_system" title="Additional member system">additional member system</a>) resulted in no one party having an overall majority for the first three Scottish parliament elections. The pro-<a href="/wiki/Scottish_independence" title="Scottish independence">independence</a> <a href="/wiki/Scottish_National_Party" title="Scottish National Party">Scottish National Party</a> led by <a href="/wiki/Alex_Salmond" title="Alex Salmond">Alex Salmond</a> achieved an overall majority in the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament_election" class="mw-redirect" title="Scottish Parliament election">2011 election</a>, winning 69 of the 129 seats available.<sup id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-127">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> The success of the SNP in achieving a majority in the Scottish Parliament paved the way for the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_independence_referendum,_2014" class="mw-redirect" title="Scottish independence referendum, 2014">September 2014 referendum on Scottish independence</a>. The majority voted against the proposition, with 55% voting no to independence.<sup id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-128">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup> More powers, particularly in relation to taxation, were devolved to the Scottish Parliament after the referendum, following cross-party talks in the <a href="/wiki/Smith_Commission" title="Smith Commission">Smith Commission</a>.
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Geography_and_natural_history">Geography and natural history</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Geography_of_Scotland" title="Geography of Scotland">Geography of Scotland</a></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Iona_Aerial_05.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Iona_Aerial_05.jpg/220px-Iona_Aerial_05.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Iona_Aerial_05.jpg/330px-Iona_Aerial_05.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Iona_Aerial_05.jpg/440px-Iona_Aerial_05.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5472" data-file-height="3648" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Iona_Aerial_05.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Iona" title="Iona">Iona</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Inner_Hebrides" title="Inner Hebrides">Inner Hebrides</a></div></div></div>
<p>The mainland of Scotland comprises the northern third of the land mass of the island of Great Britain, which lies off the north-west coast of <a href="/wiki/Continental_Europe" title="Continental Europe">Continental Europe</a>. The total area is 30,414 square miles (78,772&#160;km<sup>2</sup>),<sup id="cite_ref-Whitaker_129-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Whitaker-129">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup> comparable to the size of the Czech Republic. Scotland's only land border is with England, and runs for 60 miles (96&#160;km) between the basin of the <a href="/wiki/River_Tweed" title="River Tweed">River Tweed</a> on the east coast and the <a href="/wiki/Solway_Firth" title="Solway Firth">Solway Firth</a> in the west. The Atlantic Ocean borders the west coast and the <a href="/wiki/North_Sea" title="North Sea">North Sea</a> is to the east. The island of Ireland lies only 13 miles (21&#160;km) from the south-western peninsula of <a href="/wiki/Kintyre" title="Kintyre">Kintyre</a>;<sup id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-130">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup> Norway is 190 miles (305&#160;km) to the east and the <a href="/wiki/Faroe_Islands" title="Faroe Islands">Faroe Islands</a>, 168 miles (270&#160;km) to the north.
</p><p>The territorial extent of Scotland is generally that established by the 1237 <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_York" title="Treaty of York">Treaty of York</a> between Scotland and the Kingdom of England<sup id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-131">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> and the 1266 <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Perth" title="Treaty of Perth">Treaty of Perth</a> between Scotland and Norway.<sup id="cite_ref-Mackie_24-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Mackie-24">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup> Important exceptions include the <a href="/wiki/Isle_of_Man" title="Isle of Man">Isle of Man</a>, which having been lost to England in the 14th century is now a <a href="/wiki/Crown_dependency" class="mw-redirect" title="Crown dependency">crown dependency</a> outside of the United Kingdom; the island groups <a href="/wiki/Orkney" title="Orkney">Orkney</a> and <a href="/wiki/Shetland" title="Shetland">Shetland</a>, which were acquired from Norway in 1472;<sup id="cite_ref-Whitaker_129-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Whitaker-129">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Berwick-upon-Tweed" title="Berwick-upon-Tweed">Berwick-upon-Tweed</a>, lost to England in 1482
</p><p>The geographical <a href="/wiki/Centre_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Centre of Scotland">centre of Scotland</a> lies a few miles from the village of <a href="/wiki/Newtonmore" title="Newtonmore">Newtonmore</a> in <a href="/wiki/Badenoch" title="Badenoch">Badenoch</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-132">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup> Rising to 1,344 metres (4,409&#160;ft) above sea level, Scotland's highest point is the summit of <a href="/wiki/Ben_Nevis" title="Ben Nevis">Ben Nevis</a>, in <a href="/wiki/Lochaber" title="Lochaber">Lochaber</a>, while Scotland's longest river, the <a href="/wiki/River_Tay" title="River Tay">River Tay</a>, flows for a distance of 118 miles (190&#160;km).<sup id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-133">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-134">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Geology_and_geomorphology">Geology and geomorphology</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Geology_of_Scotland" title="Geology of Scotland">Geology of Scotland</a></div><div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:292px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg/290px-Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg" decoding="async" width="290" height="109" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg/435px-Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg/580px-Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6896" data-file-height="2586" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Gruinard_Bay_Panorama_-_October_15th_2012.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Gruinard_Bay" title="Gruinard Bay">Gruinard Bay</a></div></div></div><p>The whole of Scotland was covered by ice sheets during the <a href="/wiki/Pleistocene" title="Pleistocene">Pleistocene</a> <a href="/wiki/Ice_ages" class="mw-redirect" title="Ice ages">ice ages</a> and the landscape is much affected by glaciation. From a geological perspective, the country has three main sub-divisions.
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Highlands_and_Islands" title="Highlands and Islands">Highlands and Islands</a> lie to the north and west of the <a href="/wiki/Highland_Boundary_Fault" title="Highland Boundary Fault">Highland Boundary Fault</a>, which runs from <a href="/wiki/Isle_of_Arran" title="Isle of Arran">Arran</a> to <a href="/wiki/Stonehaven" title="Stonehaven">Stonehaven</a>. This part of Scotland largely comprises ancient rocks from the <a href="/wiki/Cambrian" title="Cambrian">Cambrian</a> and <a href="/wiki/Precambrian" title="Precambrian">Precambrian</a>, which were uplifted during the later <a href="/wiki/Caledonian_orogeny" title="Caledonian orogeny">Caledonian orogeny</a>. It is interspersed with <a href="/wiki/Igneous" class="mw-redirect" title="Igneous">igneous</a> intrusions of a more recent age, remnants of which formed mountain massifs such as the <a href="/wiki/Cairngorms" title="Cairngorms">Cairngorms</a> and <a href="/wiki/Skye" class="mw-redirect" title="Skye">Skye</a> <a href="/wiki/Cuillins" class="mw-redirect" title="Cuillins">Cuillins</a>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (November 2021)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> In north-eastern mainland Scotland <a href="/wiki/Weathering" title="Weathering">weathering</a> of rock that occurred before the <a href="/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period" title="Last Glacial Period">Last Ice Age</a> has shaped much of the landscape.<sup id="cite_ref-Hall1986_135-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Hall1986-135">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:292px;"><a href="/wiki/File:GlenfinnanShiel.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/GlenfinnanShiel.jpg/290px-GlenfinnanShiel.jpg" decoding="async" width="290" height="93" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/GlenfinnanShiel.jpg/435px-GlenfinnanShiel.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/GlenfinnanShiel.jpg/580px-GlenfinnanShiel.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5385" data-file-height="1730" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:GlenfinnanShiel.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>The <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Highlands" title="Scottish Highlands">Scottish Highlands</a>, located in the north and west of Scotland</div></div></div>
<p>A significant exception to the above are the fossil-bearing beds of <a href="/wiki/Old_Red_Sandstone" title="Old Red Sandstone">Old Red Sandstones</a> found principally along the <a href="/wiki/Moray_Firth" title="Moray Firth">Moray Firth</a> coast. The <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Highlands" title="Scottish Highlands">Highlands</a> are generally mountainous and the highest elevations in the British Isles are found here. Scotland has over 790 islands divided into four main groups: <a href="/wiki/Shetland" title="Shetland">Shetland</a>, <a href="/wiki/Orkney" title="Orkney">Orkney</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Inner_Hebrides" title="Inner Hebrides">Inner Hebrides</a> and <a href="/wiki/Outer_Hebrides" title="Outer Hebrides">Outer Hebrides</a>. There are numerous bodies of freshwater including <a href="/wiki/Loch_Lomond" title="Loch Lomond">Loch Lomond</a> and <a href="/wiki/Loch_Ness" title="Loch Ness">Loch Ness</a>. Some parts of the coastline consist of <a href="/wiki/Machair_(geography)" class="mw-redirect" title="Machair (geography)">machair</a>, a low-lying dune pasture land.
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Central_Lowlands" title="Central Lowlands">Central Lowlands</a> is a <a href="/wiki/Rift_valley" title="Rift valley">rift valley</a> mainly comprising <a href="/wiki/Paleozoic" title="Paleozoic">Paleozoic</a> formations. Many of these sediments have economic significance for it is here that the coal and iron bearing rocks that fuelled Scotland's <a href="/wiki/Industrial_revolution" class="mw-redirect" title="Industrial revolution">industrial revolution</a> are found. This area has also experienced intense volcanism, <a href="/wiki/Arthur%27s_Seat" title="Arthur&#39;s Seat">Arthur's Seat</a> in Edinburgh being the remnant of a once much larger volcano. This area is relatively low-lying, although even here hills such as the <a href="/wiki/Ochil_Hills" title="Ochil Hills">Ochils</a> and <a href="/wiki/Campsie_Fells" title="Campsie Fells">Campsie Fells</a> are rarely far from view.
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Southern_Uplands" title="Southern Uplands">Southern Uplands</a> are a range of hills almost 125 miles (200&#160;km) long, interspersed with broad valleys. They lie south of a second <a href="/wiki/Fault_(geology)" title="Fault (geology)">fault line</a> (the Southern Uplands fault) that runs from <a href="/wiki/Girvan" title="Girvan">Girvan</a> to <a href="/wiki/Dunbar" title="Dunbar">Dunbar</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-136">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-137">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Scotland_Today_»_ITKT_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Scotland_Today_»_ITKT-138">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> The geological foundations largely comprise <a href="/wiki/Silurian" title="Silurian">Silurian</a> deposits laid down some 400 to 500&#160;million years ago. The high point of the Southern Uplands is <a href="/wiki/Merrick,_Galloway" class="mw-redirect" title="Merrick, Galloway">Merrick</a> with an elevation of 843&#160;m (2,766&#160;ft).<sup id="cite_ref-Keay_23-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keay-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-139" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-139">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-140" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-140">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-141" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-141">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup> The Southern Uplands is home to Scotland's highest village, <a href="/wiki/Wanlockhead" title="Wanlockhead">Wanlockhead</a> (430&#160;m or 1,411&#160;ft above sea level).<sup id="cite_ref-Scotland_Today_»_ITKT_138-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Scotland_Today_»_ITKT-138">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Climate">Climate</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Climate_of_Scotland" title="Climate of Scotland">Climate of Scotland</a></div>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Traigh_Bail,_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Traigh_Bail%2C_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg/220px-Traigh_Bail%2C_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Traigh_Bail%2C_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg/330px-Traigh_Bail%2C_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Traigh_Bail%2C_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg/440px-Traigh_Bail%2C_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="480" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Traigh_Bail,_Tiree_-_geograph.org.uk_-_7983.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Tiree" title="Tiree">Tiree</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Inner_Hebrides" title="Inner Hebrides">Inner Hebrides</a> is one of the sunniest locations in Scotland.</div></div></div>
<p>The climate of most of Scotland is <a href="/wiki/Temperate" class="mw-redirect" title="Temperate">temperate</a> and <a href="/wiki/Oceanic_climate" title="Oceanic climate">oceanic</a>, and tends to be very changeable. As it is warmed by the <a href="/wiki/Gulf_Stream" title="Gulf Stream">Gulf Stream</a> from the Atlantic, it has much milder winters (but cooler, wetter summers) than areas on similar latitudes, such as <a href="/wiki/Labrador" title="Labrador">Labrador</a>, southern <a href="/wiki/Scandinavia" title="Scandinavia">Scandinavia</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Moscow_region" class="mw-redirect" title="Moscow region">Moscow region</a> in <a href="/wiki/Russia" title="Russia">Russia</a>, and the <a href="/wiki/Kamchatka_Peninsula" title="Kamchatka Peninsula">Kamchatka Peninsula</a> on the opposite side of <a href="/wiki/Eurasia" title="Eurasia">Eurasia</a>. Temperatures are generally lower than in the rest of the UK, with the temperature of −27.2&#160;°C (−17.0&#160;°F) recorded at <a href="/wiki/Braemar" title="Braemar">Braemar</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Grampian_Mountains" title="Grampian Mountains">Grampian Mountains</a>, on 11 February 1895, the coldest ever recorded anywhere in the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-142" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-142">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup> Winter maxima average 6&#160;°C (43&#160;°F) in the Lowlands, with summer maxima averaging 18&#160;°C (64&#160;°F). The highest temperature recorded was 35.1&#160;°C (95.2&#160;°F) at <a href="/wiki/Floors_Castle" title="Floors Castle">Floors Castle</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Borders" title="Scottish Borders">Scottish Borders</a> on 19 July 2022.<sup id="cite_ref-143" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-143">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The west of Scotland is usually warmer than the east, owing to the influence of Atlantic <a href="/wiki/Ocean_currents" class="mw-redirect" title="Ocean currents">ocean currents</a> and the colder surface temperatures of the <a href="/wiki/North_Sea" title="North Sea">North Sea</a>. <a href="/wiki/Tiree" title="Tiree">Tiree</a>, in the Inner Hebrides, is one of the sunniest places in the country: it had more than 300 hours of sunshine in May 1975.<sup id="cite_ref-Metext_144-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Metext-144">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup> Rainfall varies widely across Scotland. The western highlands of Scotland are the wettest, with annual rainfall in a few places exceeding 3,000&#160;mm (120&#160;in).<sup id="cite_ref-145" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-145">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup> In comparison, much of lowland Scotland receives less than 800&#160;mm (31&#160;in) annually.<sup id="cite_ref-Meteast_146-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Meteast-146">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup> Heavy snowfall is not common in the lowlands, but becomes more common with altitude. Braemar has an average of 59 snow days per year,<sup id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-147">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup> while many coastal areas average fewer than 10 days of lying snow per year.<sup id="cite_ref-Meteast_146-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Meteast-146">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Flora_and_fauna">Flora and fauna</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Fauna_of_Scotland" title="Fauna of Scotland">Fauna of Scotland</a> and <a href="/wiki/Flora_of_Scotland" title="Flora of Scotland">Flora of Scotland</a></div>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:RedDeerStag.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/RedDeerStag.jpg/220px-RedDeerStag.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="153" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/RedDeerStag.jpg/330px-RedDeerStag.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/RedDeerStag.jpg/440px-RedDeerStag.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3727" data-file-height="2585" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:RedDeerStag.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/Red_deer" title="Red deer">Red deer</a> <a href="/wiki/Stag" class="mw-redirect" title="Stag">stag</a> with velvet antlers in <a href="/wiki/Glen_Torridon" class="mw-redirect" title="Glen Torridon">Glen Torridon</a></div></div></div>
<p>Scotland's wildlife is typical of the north-west of Europe, although several of the larger mammals such as the lynx, brown bear, wolf, elk and walrus were hunted to extinction in historic times. There are important populations of seals and internationally significant nesting grounds for a variety of seabirds such as <a href="/wiki/Northern_gannet" title="Northern gannet">gannets</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-148" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-148">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Golden_eagle" title="Golden eagle">golden eagle</a> is something of a national icon.<sup id="cite_ref-149" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-149">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg/220px-Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="244" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg/330px-Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg/440px-Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg 2x" data-file-width="903" data-file-height="1000" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Fratercula_arctica_and_Uria_aalge_-Scotland-8.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Atlantic Puffin and Common Murre (also known as Common Guillemot) on <a href="/wiki/Lunga,_Firth_of_Lorn" title="Lunga, Firth of Lorn">Lunga</a>, <a href="/wiki/Treshnish_Isles" title="Treshnish Isles">Treshnish Isles</a></div></div></div>
<p>On the high mountain tops, species including <a href="/wiki/Rock_ptarmigan" title="Rock ptarmigan">ptarmigan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Mountain_hare" title="Mountain hare">mountain hare</a> and <a href="/wiki/Stoat" title="Stoat">stoat</a> can be seen in their white colour phase during winter months.<sup id="cite_ref-150" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-150">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup> Remnants of the native <a href="/wiki/Scots_pine" class="mw-redirect" title="Scots pine">Scots pine</a> forest exist<sup id="cite_ref-151" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-151">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup> and within these areas the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_crossbill" title="Scottish crossbill">Scottish crossbill</a>, the UK's only <a href="/wiki/Endemism" title="Endemism">endemic</a> bird species and <a href="/wiki/Vertebrate" title="Vertebrate">vertebrate</a>, can be found alongside <a href="/wiki/Western_capercaillie" title="Western capercaillie">capercaillie</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scottish_wildcat" title="Scottish wildcat">Scottish wildcat</a>, <a href="/wiki/Red_squirrel" title="Red squirrel">red squirrel</a> and <a href="/wiki/Pine_marten" class="mw-redirect" title="Pine marten">pine marten</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-152" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-152">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-153" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-153">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-154" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-154">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup> Various animals have been re-introduced, including the <a href="/wiki/White-tailed_eagle" title="White-tailed eagle">white-tailed eagle</a> in 1975, the <a href="/wiki/Red_kite" title="Red kite">red kite</a> in the 1980s,<sup id="cite_ref-155" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-155">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-156" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-156">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup> and there have been experimental projects involving the <a href="/wiki/European_beaver" class="mw-redirect" title="European beaver">beaver</a> and <a href="/wiki/Wild_boar" title="Wild boar">wild boar</a>. Today, much of the remaining native <a href="/wiki/Caledonian_Forest" title="Caledonian Forest">Caledonian Forest</a> lies within the <a href="/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park" title="Cairngorms National Park">Cairngorms National Park</a> and remnants of the forest remain at 84 locations across Scotland. On the west coast, remnants of ancient Celtic Rainforest still remain, particularly on the Taynish peninsula in <a href="/wiki/Argyll" title="Argyll">Argyll</a>, these forests are particularly rare due to high rates of deforestation throughout Scottish history.<sup id="cite_ref-157" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-157">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BBC_News_158-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BBC_News-158">&#91;158&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The flora of the country is varied incorporating both <a href="/wiki/Deciduous" title="Deciduous">deciduous</a> and <a href="/wiki/Coniferous" class="mw-redirect" title="Coniferous">coniferous</a> woodland as well as <a href="/wiki/Moorland" title="Moorland">moorland</a> and <a href="/wiki/Tundra" title="Tundra">tundra</a> species. Large-scale commercial tree planting and management of upland moorland habitat for the grazing of sheep and <a href="/wiki/Field_sports" title="Field sports">field sport</a> activities like <a href="/wiki/Deer_stalking" title="Deer stalking">deer stalking</a> and <a href="/wiki/Driven_grouse_shooting" title="Driven grouse shooting">driven grouse shooting</a> impacts the distribution of <a href="/wiki/Indigenous_(ecology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Indigenous (ecology)">indigenous</a> plants and animals.<sup id="cite_ref-159" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-159">&#91;159&#93;</a></sup> The UK's tallest tree is a <a href="/wiki/Abies_grandis" title="Abies grandis">grand fir</a> planted beside <a href="/wiki/Loch_Fyne" title="Loch Fyne">Loch Fyne</a>, Argyll in the 1870s, and the <a href="/wiki/Fortingall_Yew" title="Fortingall Yew">Fortingall Yew</a> may be 5,000 years old and is probably the oldest living thing in Europe.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy_dispute#Disputed_statement" title="Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute"><span title="The material near this tag is possibly inaccurate or nonfactual. (April 2017)">dubious</span></a>&#32;<span class="metadata"> &#8211; <a href="/wiki/Talk:Scotland#Dubious" title="Talk:Scotland">discuss</a></span></i>&#93;</sup><sup id="cite_ref-160" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-160">&#91;160&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-161" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-161">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-162" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-162">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup> Although the number of native <a href="/wiki/Vascular_plant" title="Vascular plant">vascular plants</a> is low by world standards, Scotland's substantial <a href="/wiki/Bryophyte" title="Bryophyte">bryophyte</a> flora is of global importance.<sup id="cite_ref-163" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-163">&#91;163&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-RBGE_164-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-RBGE-164">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Demographics">Demographics</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Demography_of_Scotland" title="Demography of Scotland">Demography of Scotland</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Languages_of_Scotland" title="Languages of Scotland">Languages of Scotland</a>, <a href="/wiki/Religion_in_Scotland" title="Religion in Scotland">Religion in Scotland</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Scottish_people" title="Scottish people">Scottish people</a></div>
<p>The population of Scotland at the 2001 Census was 5,062,011. This rose to 5,295,400, the highest ever, at the 2011 Census.<sup id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_165-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-165">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup> The most recent ONS estimate, for mid-2019, was 5,463,300.<sup id="cite_ref-ONS-pop-ests-June2018_12-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ONS-pop-ests-June2018-12">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:Scotland_population_cartogram.svg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Scotland_population_cartogram.svg/220px-Scotland_population_cartogram.svg.png" decoding="async" width="220" height="354" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Scotland_population_cartogram.svg/330px-Scotland_population_cartogram.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Scotland_population_cartogram.svg/440px-Scotland_population_cartogram.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="512" data-file-height="823" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:Scotland_population_cartogram.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Scotland population <a href="/wiki/Cartogram" title="Cartogram">cartogram</a>. The size of councils is in proportion to their population.</div></div></div>
<p>In the 2011 Census, 62% of Scotland's population stated their <a href="/wiki/National_identity" title="National identity">national identity</a> as '<a href="/wiki/Scottish_people" title="Scottish people">Scottish</a> only', 18% as 'Scottish and British', 8% as 'British only', and 4% chose 'other identity only'.<sup id="cite_ref-166" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-166">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Although <a href="/wiki/Edinburgh" title="Edinburgh">Edinburgh</a> is the capital of Scotland, the largest city is Glasgow, which has just over 584,000 inhabitants. The <a href="/wiki/Greater_Glasgow" title="Greater Glasgow">Greater Glasgow</a> conurbation, with a population of almost 1.2&#160;million, is home to nearly a quarter of Scotland's population.<sup id="cite_ref-167" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-167">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Central_Belt" title="Central Belt">Central Belt</a> is where most of the main towns and cities are located, including Glasgow, Edinburgh, Dundee, and Perth. Scotland's only major city outside the Central Belt is Aberdeen. The <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Lowlands" title="Scottish Lowlands">Scottish Lowlands</a> host 80% of the total population, where the <a href="/wiki/Central_Belt" title="Central Belt">Central Belt</a> accounts for 3.5&#160;million people.
</p><p>In general, only the more accessible and larger islands remain inhabited. Currently, fewer than 90 remain inhabited. The Southern Uplands are essentially rural in nature and dominated by agriculture and forestry.<sup id="cite_ref-168" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-168">&#91;168&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-169" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-169">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup> Because of housing problems in Glasgow and Edinburgh, <a href="/wiki/New_towns_in_the_United_Kingdom#Scotland" title="New towns in the United Kingdom">five new towns</a> were designated between 1947 and 1966. They are <a href="/wiki/East_Kilbride" title="East Kilbride">East Kilbride</a>, <a href="/wiki/Glenrothes" title="Glenrothes">Glenrothes</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cumbernauld" title="Cumbernauld">Cumbernauld</a>, <a href="/wiki/Livingston,_West_Lothian" title="Livingston, West Lothian">Livingston</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Irvine,_North_Ayrshire" title="Irvine, North Ayrshire">Irvine</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-170" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-170">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Immigration since World War II has given Glasgow, Edinburgh, and Dundee small South Asian communities.<sup id="cite_ref-171" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-171">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup> In 2011, there were an estimated 49,000 ethnically Pakistani people living in Scotland, making them the largest non-White ethnic group.<sup id="cite_ref-ethnicity_172-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ethnicity-172">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup> Since the <a href="/wiki/Enlargement_of_the_European_Union" title="Enlargement of the European Union">enlargement of the European Union</a> more people from <a href="/wiki/Central_Europe" title="Central Europe">Central</a> and Eastern Europe have moved to Scotland, and the 2011 census indicated that 61,000 <a href="/wiki/Poles" title="Poles">Poles</a> live there.<sup id="cite_ref-ethnicity_172-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ethnicity-172">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-173" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-173">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Scotland has three officially recognised languages: English, <a href="/wiki/Scots_language" title="Scots language">Scots</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Gaelic" title="Scottish Gaelic">Scottish Gaelic</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-174">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-175">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup> Scottish Standard English, a variety of English as spoken in Scotland, is at one end of a bipolar <a href="/wiki/Linguistic_continuum" class="mw-redirect" title="Linguistic continuum">linguistic continuum</a>, with broad <a href="/wiki/Scots_language" title="Scots language">Scots</a> at the other.<sup id="cite_ref-176" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-176">&#91;176&#93;</a></sup> Scottish Standard English may have been influenced to varying degrees by Scots.<sup id="cite_ref-Stuart-Smith_J._2008._p.48_177-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Stuart-Smith_J._2008._p.48-177">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-178">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup> The 2011 census indicated that 63% of the population had "no skills in Scots".<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup> Others speak <a href="/wiki/Highland_English" title="Highland English">Highland English</a>. Gaelic is mostly spoken in the <a href="/wiki/Western_Isles" class="mw-redirect" title="Western Isles">Western Isles</a>, where a large proportion of people still speak it. Nationally, its use is confined to 1% of the population.<sup id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-180">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup> The number of Gaelic speakers in Scotland dropped from 250,000 in 1881 to 60,000 in 2008.<sup id="cite_ref-181" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-181">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>There are many more people with Scottish ancestry living abroad than the total population of Scotland. In the 2000 Census, 9.2&#160;million Americans self-reported some degree of <a href="/wiki/Scottish_American" class="mw-redirect" title="Scottish American">Scottish</a> descent.<sup id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-182">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Ulster" title="Ulster">Ulster</a>'s Protestant population is mainly of lowland Scottish descent,<sup id="cite_ref-183" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-183">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup> and it is estimated that there are more than 27&#160;million descendants of the <a href="/wiki/Ulster_Scots_people" title="Ulster Scots people">Scots-Irish</a> migration now living in the US.<sup id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-184">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-185">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup> In Canada, the <a href="/wiki/Scottish-Canadian" class="mw-redirect" title="Scottish-Canadian">Scottish-Canadian</a> community accounts for 4.7&#160;million people.<sup id="cite_ref-cancensus_186-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cancensus-186">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup> About 20% of the original European settler population of New Zealand came from Scotland.<sup id="cite_ref-187" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-187">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August 2012, the Scottish population reached an all-time high of 5.25&#160;million people.<sup id="cite_ref-thecourier1_188-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-thecourier1-188">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup> The reasons given were that, in Scotland, births were outnumbering the number of deaths, and immigrants were moving to Scotland from overseas. In 2011, 43,700 people moved from Wales, Northern Ireland or England to live in Scotland.<sup id="cite_ref-thecourier1_188-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-thecourier1-188">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Total_fertility_rate" title="Total fertility rate">total fertility rate</a> (TFR) in Scotland is below the replacement rate of 2.1 (the TFR was 1.73 in 2011<sup id="cite_ref-189" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-189">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup>). The majority of births are to unmarried women (51.3% of births were outside of marriage in 2012<sup id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-190">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup>).
</p><p>Life expectancy for those born in Scotland between 2012 and 2014 is 77.1 years for males and 81.1 years for females.<sup id="cite_ref-life_expectancy_2015_191-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-life_expectancy_2015-191">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup> This is the lowest of any of the four countries of the UK.<sup id="cite_ref-life_expectancy_2015_191-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-life_expectancy_2015-191">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup>
</p>

<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Religion">Religion</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Religion_in_Scotland" title="Religion in Scotland">Religion in Scotland</a></div>
<div class="thumb tleft"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><a href="/wiki/File:St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg/220px-St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg/330px-St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg/440px-St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="685" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:St.Giles_Cathedral_-_panoramio.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div><a href="/wiki/St_Giles%27_Cathedral" title="St Giles&#39; Cathedral">St Giles' Cathedral</a>, a parish church of the <a href="/wiki/Church_of_Scotland" title="Church of Scotland">Church of Scotland</a>, Edinburgh</div></div></div>
<p>In 2011 just over half (54%) of the Scottish population reported being a <a href="/wiki/Christianity" title="Christianity">Christian</a> while nearly 37% reported not having a religion in a 2011 census.<sup id="cite_ref-2011_census_religion_193-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2011_census_religion-193">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup>
Since the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Reformation" title="Scottish Reformation">Scottish Reformation</a> of 1560, the <a href="/wiki/National_church" title="National church">national church</a> (the <a href="/wiki/Church_of_Scotland" title="Church of Scotland">Church of Scotland</a>, also known as <a href="/wiki/Kirk" title="Kirk">The Kirk</a>) has been <a href="/wiki/Protestant" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant">Protestant</a> in classification and <a href="/wiki/Reformed_theology" class="mw-redirect" title="Reformed theology">Reformed</a> in theology. Since 1689 it has had a <a href="/wiki/Presbyterian" class="mw-redirect" title="Presbyterian">Presbyterian</a> system of church government and enjoys independence from the state.<sup id="cite_ref-Keay_23-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Keay-23">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup> Its membership dropped just below 300,000 in 2020 (5% of the total population) <sup id="cite_ref-194" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-194">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-scotsman.com_195-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-scotsman.com-195">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-196" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-196">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup> The Church operates a territorial parish structure, with every community in Scotland having a local congregation.
</p><p>Scotland also has a significant <a href="/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church_in_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Catholic Church in Scotland">Roman Catholic</a> population, 19% professing that faith, particularly in Greater Glasgow and the north-west.<sup id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-197">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup> After the Reformation, Roman Catholicism in Scotland continued in the Highlands and some western islands like <a href="/wiki/Uist" title="Uist">Uist</a> and <a href="/wiki/Barra" title="Barra">Barra</a>, and it was strengthened during the 19th century by immigration from Ireland. Other Christian denominations in Scotland include the <a href="/wiki/Free_Church_of_Scotland_(since_1900)" title="Free Church of Scotland (since 1900)">Free Church of Scotland</a>, and various other Presbyterian offshoots. Scotland's third largest church is the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Episcopal_Church" title="Scottish Episcopal Church">Scottish Episcopal Church</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-198" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-198">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>There are an estimated 75,000 Muslims in Scotland (about 1.4% of the population),<sup id="cite_ref-2011_census_religion_193-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2011_census_religion-193">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-GROSCOT_199-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GROSCOT-199">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup> and significant but smaller <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Scotland" title="History of the Jews in Scotland">Jewish</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hinduism_in_Scotland" title="Hinduism in Scotland">Hindu</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sikh" class="mw-redirect" title="Sikh">Sikh</a> communities, especially in Glasgow.<sup id="cite_ref-GROSCOT_199-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-GROSCOT-199">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Samy%C3%A9_Ling" class="mw-redirect" title="Samyé Ling">Samyé Ling</a> monastery near <a href="/wiki/Eskdalemuir" title="Eskdalemuir">Eskdalemuir</a>, which celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2007, is the first <a href="/wiki/Buddhism" title="Buddhism">Buddhist</a> monastery in western Europe.<sup id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-200">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Politics_and_government">Politics and government</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"/><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Politics_of_Scotland" title="Politics of Scotland">Politics of Scotland</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament" title="Scottish Parliament">Scottish Parliament</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Government" title="Scottish Government">Scottish Government</a></div>

srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Official_portrait_of_First_Minister%2C_Nicola_Sturgeon.jpg/248px-Official_portrait_of_First_Minister%2C_Nicola_Sturgeon.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Official_portrait_of_First_Minister%2C_Nicola_Sturgeon.jpg/330px-Official_portrait_of_First_Minister%2C_Nicola_Sturgeon.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="1678" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Nicola_Sturgeon" title="Nicola Sturgeon">Nicola Sturgeon</a><br /><a href="/wiki/First_Minister_of_Scotland" title="First Minister of Scotland">First Minister</a><br />since 2014</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>The head of state of the United Kingdom is the monarch, who is <a href="/wiki/King_Charles_III" class="mw-redirect" title="King Charles III">King Charles III</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-201" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-201">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> The monarchy of the United Kingdom continues to use a variety of styles, titles and other royal symbols of statehood specific to pre-union Scotland, including: the <a href="/wiki/Royal_Standard_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal Standard of Scotland">Royal Standard of Scotland</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Royal_coat_of_arms_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Royal coat of arms of the United Kingdom">Royal coat of arms</a> used in Scotland together with its associated <a href="/wiki/Royal_Standard_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Royal Standard of the United Kingdom">Royal Standard</a>, royal titles including that of <a href="/wiki/Duke_of_Rothesay" title="Duke of Rothesay">Duke of Rothesay</a>, certain <a href="/wiki/Great_Officer_of_State" class="mw-redirect" title="Great Officer of State">Great Officers of State</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Chivalric_order" class="mw-redirect" title="Chivalric order">chivalric</a> <a href="/wiki/Order_of_the_Thistle" title="Order of the Thistle">Order of the Thistle</a> and, since 1999, reinstating a ceremonial role for the <a href="/wiki/Crown_of_Scotland" title="Crown of Scotland">Crown of Scotland</a> after a 292-year hiatus.<sup id="cite_ref-202" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-202">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_II" class="mw-redirect" title="Queen Elizabeth II">Queen Elizabeth II</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Regnal_number" title="Regnal number">regnal numbering</a> caused <a href="/wiki/List_of_titles_and_honours_of_Elizabeth_II#Royal_titles_and_styles" title="List of titles and honours of Elizabeth II">controversy</a> in 1953 because there had never been an Elizabeth I in Scotland. <a href="/wiki/MacCormick_v_Lord_Advocate" title="MacCormick v Lord Advocate">MacCormick v Lord Advocate</a> was a legal action was brought in Scotland's <a href="/wiki/Court_of_Session" title="Court of Session">Court of Session</a> by the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Covenant_Association" title="Scottish Covenant Association">Scottish Covenant Association</a> to contest the right of the Queen to entitle herself "Elizabeth II" within Scotland, but <a href="/wiki/Monarchy_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Monarchy of the United Kingdom">the Crown</a> won the appeal against the case's dismissal, since as royal titulature was legislated for by the Royal Titles Act 1953 and a matter of <a href="/wiki/Royal_prerogative_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Royal prerogative in the United Kingdom">royal prerogative</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-203" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-203">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Scotland has limited <a href="/wiki/Self-government" class="mw-redirect" title="Self-government">self-government</a> within the United Kingdom, as well as representation in the British Parliament. Executive and legislative powers respectively have been devolved to the Scottish Government and the Scottish Parliament at <a href="/wiki/Holyrood,_Edinburgh" title="Holyrood, Edinburgh">Holyrood</a> in Edinburgh since 1999. The British Parliament retains control over <a href="/wiki/Reserved_and_excepted_matters" class="mw-redirect" title="Reserved and excepted matters">reserved matters</a> specified in the <a href="/wiki/Scotland_Act_1998" title="Scotland Act 1998">Scotland Act 1998</a>, including taxes, social security, defence, international relations and broadcasting.<sup id="cite_ref-Gate_204-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Gate-204">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup> The Scottish Parliament has legislative authority for all other areas relating to Scotland. It initially had only a limited power to <a href="/wiki/Scottish_variable_rate" title="Scottish variable rate">vary income tax</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-205" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-205">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup> but powers over taxation and social security were significantly expanded by the Scotland Acts of <a href="/wiki/Scotland_Act_2012" title="Scotland Act 2012">2012</a> and <a href="/wiki/Scotland_Act_2016" title="Scotland Act 2016">2016</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-206" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-206">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup> The 2016 Act gave the Scottish Government powers to manage the affairs of the <a href="/wiki/Crown_Estate" title="Crown Estate">Crown Estate</a> in Scotland, leading to the creation of <a href="/wiki/Crown_Estate_Scotland" title="Crown Estate Scotland">Crown Estate Scotland</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-207">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Scottish Parliament can give legislative consent over devolved matters back to the British Parliament by passing a <a href="/wiki/Legislative_Consent_Motion" class="mw-redirect" title="Legislative Consent Motion">Legislative Consent Motion</a> if United Kingdom-wide legislation is considered more appropriate for a certain issue. The programmes of legislation enacted by the Scottish Parliament have seen a divergence in the provision of public services compared to the rest of the UK. For instance, university education and some care services for the elderly are free at point of use in Scotland, while fees are paid in the rest of the UK. Scotland was the first country in the UK to ban smoking in enclosed public places.<sup id="cite_ref-208" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-208">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"/><div class="thumb tmulti tleft"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:204px;max-width:204px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:Bute_House,_Charlotte_Square_Edinburgh.JPG" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption text-align-center"><a href="/wiki/Bute_House" title="Bute House">Bute House</a> is the official residence and workplace of the first minister.</div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><a href="/wiki/File:SPCB_-_Public_entrance_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/SPCB_-_Public_entrance_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg/200px-SPCB_-_Public_entrance_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="133" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/SPCB_-_Public_entrance_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg/300px-SPCB_-_Public_entrance_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/SPCB_-_Public_entrance_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg/400px-SPCB_-_Public_entrance_at_the_Scottish_Parliament.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4064" data-file-height="2704" /></a></div><div class="thumbcaption text-align-center"><a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament_Building" title="Scottish Parliament Building">Holyrood</a> is the seat of the national parliament of Scotland.</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>The Scottish Parliament is a <a href="/wiki/Unicameral" class="mw-redirect" title="Unicameral">unicameral</a> legislature with 129 members (MSPs): 73 of them represent individual constituencies and are elected on a <a href="/wiki/First-past-the-post" class="mw-redirect" title="First-past-the-post">first-past-the-post</a> system; the other 56 are elected in eight different electoral regions by the <a href="/wiki/Additional_member_system_(Scottish_Parliament)" class="mw-redirect" title="Additional member system (Scottish Parliament)">additional member system</a>. MSPs normally serve for a five-year period.<sup id="cite_ref-209" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-209">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup> The Parliament nominates one of its Members, who is then appointed by the monarch to serve as first minister. Other ministers are appointed by the first minister and serve at his/her discretion. Together they make up the Scottish Government, the executive arm of the devolved government.<sup id="cite_ref-210" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-210">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup> The Scottish Government is headed by the first minister, who is accountable to the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Parliament" title="Scottish Parliament">Scottish Parliament</a> and is the minister of charge of the Scottish Government. The first minister is also the political leader of Scotland. The Scottish Government also comprises the <a href="/wiki/Deputy_First_Minister_of_Scotland" title="Deputy First Minister of Scotland">deputy first minister</a>, who deputises for the first minister during a period of absence. Alongside the deputy first minister's requirements as Deputy, the minister also has a cabinet ministerial responsibility.<sup id="cite_ref-211" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-211">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Third_Sturgeon_government" title="Third Sturgeon government">current Scottish Government</a> has nine cabinet secretaries and there are 15 other ministers who work alongside the cabinet secretaries in their appointed areas.<sup id="cite_ref-ScotParliament_212-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ScotParliament-212">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In the <a href="/wiki/2021_Scottish_Parliament_election" title="2021 Scottish Parliament election">2021 election</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_National_Party" title="Scottish National Party">Scottish National Party</a> (SNP) won 64 of the 129 seats available.<sup id="cite_ref-2016_results_213-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2016_results-213">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Nicola_Sturgeon" title="Nicola Sturgeon">Nicola Sturgeon</a>, the leader of the SNP, has been the first minister since November 2014.<sup id="cite_ref-214" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-214">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Conservatives" title="Scottish Conservatives">Scottish Conservatives</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Labour" title="Scottish Labour">Scottish Labour</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Liberal_Democrats" title="Scottish Liberal Democrats">Scottish Liberal Democrats</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Scottish_Greens" title="Scottish Greens">Scottish Greens</a> also have representation in the Parliament.<sup id="cite_ref-2016_results_213-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2016_results-213">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Next_Scottish_Parliament_election" title="Next Scottish Parliament election">next Scottish Parliament election</a> is due to be held on 7 May 2026.<sup id="cite_ref-215" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-215">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Scotland is represented in the British <a href="/wiki/House_of_Commons" title="House of Commons">House of Commons</a> by 59 MPs elected from territory-based Scottish constituencies. In the <a href="/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2019 United Kingdom general election">2019 general election</a>, the SNP won 48 of the 59 seats.<sup id="cite_ref-2019_election_216-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2019_election-216">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> This represented a significant increase from the <a href="/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="2017 United Kingdom general election">2017 general election</a>, when the SNP won 35 seats.<sup id="cite_ref-2019_election_216-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2019_election-216">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-217" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-217">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup> Conservative, Labour and Liberal Democrat parties also represent Scottish constituencies in the House of Commons.<sup id="cite_ref-2019_election_216-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-2019_election-216">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Next_United_Kingdom_general_election" title="Next United Kingdom general election">next general election</a> is scheduled for 2 May 2024. The <a href="/wiki/Scotland_Office" class="mw-redirect" title="Scotland Office">Scotland Office</a> represents the British government in Scotland on reserved matters and represents Scottish interests within the government.<sup id="cite_ref-218" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-218">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup> The Scotland Office is led by the <a href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Scotland" title="Secretary of State for Scotland">Secretary of State for Scotland</a>, who sits in the <a href="/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Cabinet of the United Kingdom">Cabinet of the United Kingdom</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-jack_219-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jack-219">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup> Conservative MP <a href="/wiki/Alister_Jack" title="Alister Jack">Alister Jack</a> has held the position since July 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-jack_219-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jack-219">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Devolved_government_relations">Devolved government relations</span></h3>
<div class="thumb tright"><div class="thumbinner" style="width:252px;"><a href="/wiki/File:British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg" class="image"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg/250px-British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="167" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg/375px-British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg/500px-British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5557" data-file-height="3705" /></a>  <div class="thumbcaption"><div class="magnify"><a href="/wiki/File:British_Irish_Council_meeting_in_Glasgow.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></a></div>Scotland has been a member of the <a href="/wiki/British-Irish_Council" class="mw-redirect" title="British-Irish Council">British-Irish Council</a> since 1999.</div></div></div>
<p>The relationships between the central government of the UK and devolved governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are based on the extra-statutory principles and agreements with the main elements being set out in a <i>Memorandum of Understanding</i> between the British government and the devolved governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The MOU lays emphasis on the principles of good communication, consultation and co-operation.<sup id="cite_ref-220" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-220">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Since devolution in 1999, Scotland has devolved stronger working relations across the two other devolved governments, the <a href="/wiki/Welsh_Government" title="Welsh Government">Welsh Government</a> and <a href="/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Executive" title="Northern Ireland Executive">Northern Ireland Executive</a>.
